Legislation to relax U.S. export restrictions on computer encoding technology advanced as the House Judiciary Committee approved the measure.
The bill is called the Security and Freedom through Encryption Act.
The bill will be reviewed by the House International Relations Committee.
Opponents of the bill plan to contest it in the House International Relations Committee.
Encryption is a technology that scrambles information, making it unreadable without a password or software key.
The Clinton administration opposes the bill, arguing it could aid international criminals and terrorists.
Representative Bob Goodlatte is the author of the bill.
Goodlatte expressed hope for a compromise with administration officials.
The bill would criminalize the use of encryption to conceal information related to felonies.
Software industry officials and privacy advocates support the legislation and urge lawmakers to continue its progress.

The Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) issued forecasts for 1997 on Monday.
The CSU predicted a slight economic upturn for 1997.
The CSU expected real gross domestic product (GDP) growth for 1997 of 4.0-5.0 percent.
The CSU estimated GDP growth of 4.1 percent for 1996.
The CSU forecasted average annual inflation to ease to 7.5-8.0 percent from 8.8 percent.
The CSU projected the current account deficit to grow to 137-145 billion crowns from an estimated 110.6 billion crowns in 1996.
Analysts warned that the widening current account and trade deficits could undermine the economy.
David Lubin, an economist at HSBC Midland, stated that the forecasts were credible but not very encouraging.
The CSU estimated the current account shortfall to be 8.6-9.1 percent of GDP in 1997.
The CSU forecasted the trade deficit to widen to 202-212 billion crowns from a deficit of 160.3 billion crowns in 1996.

China will tighten inspections of imported animals and plants next year for possible diseases.
Chinese quarantine officials banned poultry imports from several U.S. states and a part of Britain.
The China Daily Business Weekly reported that animal and quarantine authorities will carry out stricter inspections.
Inspections will cover imports and exports of plants, animals, fruit, agricultural goods, containers, packages, and other transport materials.
New regulations approved by the State Council will govern these inspections.
Quarantine and customs officials will inspect both hand-carried items and goods imported or exported by traders.
Pets and plants of diplomats with diplomatic immunity will also be inspected.
Authorities could impose fines of up to 50,000 yuan ($6,000) on violators.
China announced a ban on poultry imports from Missouri and Oklahoma due to five cases of Newcastle disease.
The United States denied the accusation and sought talks with China to lift the ban.

USG Corp is a maker of building products such as wallboard.
USG Corp aims to double its earnings by the early 2000s from its 1995 earnings base.
William Foote is the chief executive of USG Corp.
USG Corp reported earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization of $417 million in 1995.
USG Corp's EBITDA rose to $437 million in 1996.
USG Corp plans to achieve its earnings goal through revenue growth from production expansion and cost-cutting initiatives.
USG Corp seeks to have its debt rating raised to investment grade by the end of 1998.
USG Corp currently spends about $150 million a year on capital improvements and $150 million a year to pay down debt.
USG Corp's United States Gypsum Co unit plans to spend at least $85 million to build a facility for manufacturing gypsum wood fiber panels.
USG Corp announced plans to build a new wallboard manufacturing facility in Bridgeport, Ala. for $110 million.

Chrysler Corp. announced that the base price of the redesigned 1997 Jeep Cherokee will be $555 to $1,344 higher than the 1996 model.
The base SE, two-door, two-wheel-drive 1997 Jeep Cherokee will start at $15,825, an increase of $555 from the 1996 model.
The four-door, four-wheel-drive Cherokee Sport model will sell for $20,985, an increase of $815 from the 1996 model.
The four-door, four-wheel-drive Country model will start at $23,945, an increase of $1,344 over the 1996 model.
The Sport and Country models of the 1997 Jeep Cherokee offer a standard six-cylinder engine.
The SE model of the 1997 Jeep Cherokee offers a standard four-cylinder engine.
All prices for the 1997 Jeep Cherokee include a $525 destination charge.
The 1997 Jeep Cherokee features a new instrument panel with dual air bags, updated sheet metal, and a redesigned grille.
Chrysler has the capacity to build about 150,000 Cherokees annually at its Toledo, Ohio, assembly plant.
Through the first 10 months of 1996, Jeep dealers sold 131,995 Cherokees, a 44 percent increase over the 91,246 sold in the same period of 1995.

Cascade Communications Corp reported growth in its core frame-relay business in 1996.
The growth in frame-relay business was partially concealed in other business segments.
Daniel Smith is the chief executive of Cascade Communications Corp.
Some frame-relay business is included in the sales of Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) products.
Daniel Smith expects Cascade to gain frame-relay market share in 1997, but at a slower pace than in 1996.
Cascade grew market share significantly in 1996.
Cascade's policy is not to make specific growth forecasts.
Cascade experienced relatively flat sequential frame-relay sales in the fourth quarter compared to the September quarter.
The flat sales were attributed to delays in telecom customer orders.
Cascade stock fell sharply after the release of its fourth quarter earnings, despite slightly better-than-expected results.

Nomura Securities Co reported a parent net loss of 271.51 billion yen ($2.15 billion) for the business year 1996/97.
Nomura Securities Co had a profit of 23.1 billion yen ($183 million) in the previous year, 1995/96.
The net loss for 1996/97 was largely due to a special loss of 371 billion yen ($2.94 billion) related to support for Nomura Finance Co.
Nomura Securities Co recorded a parent current profit of 124.19 billion yen ($985 million) for the year, an increase of 35.7 percent year-on-year.
The current profit reported by Nomura is pre-tax and includes gains and losses from investments.
On a group basis, Nomura reported a net loss of 91.07 billion yen ($722 million) for 1996/97.
In the previous year, Nomura had a group profit of 81.27 billion yen ($645 million) under U.S. accounting rules.
Nomura Securities Co faced a scandal involving two directors linked to illegal deals with a corporate customer associated with sokaiya.
The scandal has negatively impacted Nomura's business, leading to a decrease in trading activity from clients.
Nomura plans to reduce its monthly operating expenditures to between 20.2 billion and 20.3 billion yen (about $161 million) starting in April.

Canadian mining companies are concerned about the strengthening Canadian dollar.
Vic Wells is a spokesman for Anvil Range Mining Corp.
Anvil Range Mining Corp. suspended zinc and lead mining at its Faro property due to the stronger Canadian dollar.
Analysts forecast a surge in the Canadian currency in 1997.
Some analysts predict the Canadian dollar will rise to 80 U.S. cents from its current 74 U.S. cent range.
George Miller is the president of the Mining Association of Canada.
Canada is the world's largest producer of potash, uranium, and zinc.
Canada is the world's second biggest producer of nickel after Russia.
Companies that produce metal mainly in Canada are affected by a strengthening Canadian dollar.
Alan Thomas is the chief financial officer of Noranda Inc.

Deng Xiaoping's health is deteriorating.
Jiang Zemin and other leaders have cut short provincial trips to return to Beijing.
Jiang Zemin returned from a visit to Ganzhou in Jiangxi province.
Li Peng flew back to Beijing from a tour of Guangdong province.
Jiang Zemin and Li Peng returned to Beijing due to concerns about Deng Xiaoping's health.
Deng Xiaoping is 92 years old.
Deng Xiaoping lives in a guarded compound behind the Forbidden City in Beijing.
Diplomats indicate that the travel of top leaders reflects Deng's health status.
Chinese officials report little change in Deng's health, stating he is all right for his age.
Deng Xiaoping has not been seen in public since the 1994 Chinese Lunar New Year festival.

Scottish Hydro-Electric Plc reported lower than expected half year profits.
Scottish Hydro-Electric Plc increased its dividend by 11 percent.
Chief executive Roger Young stated the company aims to deliver dividend improvement by expanding the business.
Pretax profits for Scottish Hydro-Electric Plc decreased to 61.3 million pounds from 61.7 million pounds.
The expected range for pretax profits was between 63 million and 70.7 million pounds.
The dividend was set at 5.28 pence per share.
Scottish Hydro-Electric Plc shares decreased by 1.5 pence to 316.5 pence.
Low rainfall impacted profits, leading to increased coal usage at a cost of 6.3 million pounds.
Chairman Lord Wilson expressed confidence in an encouraging result for the full 12 month period.
Scottish Hydro-Electric Plc is the preferred bidder for a 50 percent stake in Keadby power station.

Pop singer Michael Jackson arrived in Prague on Tuesday to launch his first tour in two years.
Promoters erected a large statue of Michael Jackson on a hill in Prague.
The statue is located where a monument to Soviet chief Josef Stalin once stood.
Jackson's three-month 'HIStory' tour through Europe, Africa, and Asia begins on Saturday.
A concert on Prague's Letna Plain is expected to attract 130,000 attendees.
Jackson arrived four days early to sightsee in and around Prague.
He emerged from his jet at Prague airport's VIP terminal wearing a gold lame and red outfit.
Several hundred fans greeted Jackson at the airport, and he hugged some who presented gifts.
Jackson traveled to his hotel in a Rolls Royce, escorted by police and a convoy of luxury cars.
Thousands of fans gathered at his hotel on the river Vltava to see him.

Albright & Wilson Plc plans to focus its business on emerging markets, particularly South America, China, and India.
Robin Paul is the chief executive of Albright & Wilson.
Robin Paul stated that emerging markets are important for the growth of Albright & Wilson.
Albright & Wilson aims to expand through partnerships and acquiring majority stakes in partner companies.
Last year, Albright & Wilson took a majority stake in an Indian partner.
Albright & Wilson is increasing its activities in phosphates and surfactants in India.
Albright & Wilson announced a 13.6 percent rise in pre-tax profits for 1996.
Gabriel Kow has been appointed president of Albright & Wilson's Asia Pacific operations.
Gabriel Kow previously worked at Glaxo Wellcome Plc.
Albright & Wilson is the world's largest producer of wet phosphoric acid.

Shares in Pearson Plc gained on Wednesday.
Marjorie Scardino officially became the chief executive of Pearson Plc.
Marjorie Scardino is the first woman to head one of Britain's leading companies.
Scardino stated that Pearson's profit performance has been inadequate.
Disposals are expected as Scardino aims for greater focus on core businesses.
Pearson shares increased by 8.5p to 738.5p on Wednesday.
Scardino was previously the chief executive of The Economist Group.
Scardino spent her first day meeting employees at Pearson's central London headquarters.
Analysts expect swift action from Scardino to focus the company.
Analysts have identified Pearson's investment banking interests, theme park businesses, and Mindscape as candidates for sale.

The consortium building the Sydney 2000 Olympic stadium closed its funding scheme on Thursday.
Stadium Australia aimed to offset A$660 million in construction costs through the sale of 34,400 'Gold Passes'.
The 'Gold Passes' offered a combination of Olympic tickets, equity, and stadium membership.
Investors and sports fans did not purchase the A$364.4 million offer.
Underwriters faced a funding shortfall estimated at up to A$240 million.
This shortfall would classify it as one of Australia's biggest share flops.
Stadium Australia plans to release the results of the float late next week.
Michael Knight, president of the Sydney Organising Committee for the Olympic Games, acknowledged the float likely fell short.
The Stadium Australia offer has been open for almost six months, longer than most share offers.
The offer included 34,400 gold packages at A$10,000 each and 600 platinum passes at A$33,000 each.

Informix Corp. is facing declining sales of its database software products.
Informix Corp. needs to raise cash and refinance its leases to maintain operations.
Informix plans to raise capital to offset upcoming operational losses.
Informix is considering refinancing leases on land in Santa Clara, California.
Informix stated that there is no assurance that necessary financing will be available.
The failure to raise working capital could adversely affect Informix's business and financial condition.
Informix is based in Menlo Park, California.
Informix is the second-largest publisher of database software.
Informix reported a first-quarter loss of $140.1 million on revenue of $133.7 million.
Informix's cash supply decreased from $261 million to $120.6 million due to losses and a cash deposit.

Chinese copper producers may start selling copper to take advantage of high prices.
London Metal Exchange (LME) copper prices are near their highest level in almost a year.
Chinese producers want to sell before a predicted price correction in the international market.
A Shanghai copper trader stated that Chinese producers have begun selling domestically due to concerns about price sustainability.
Prices on the Shanghai Metal Exchange (SME) rose on Friday morning, reflecting local market fundamentals.
Shanghai copper futures opened mostly up on Friday, with the June 1996 contract opening at 23,650 yuan ($2,851) per tonne.
Traders on the SME expect copper prices to consolidate between 23,000 and 24,000 yuan ($2,771-2,891) in the short term.
LME copper prices fluctuated on Thursday, closing at $2,403 per tonne after a $28 increase.
Traders and analysts believe the LME copper price is not supported by market fundamentals.
China's total copper production in 1996 was 909,700 tonnes, a 5.71 percent increase from 1995.

Russia's oil sector experienced its smallest fall in output after a decade of declines.
Analysts predict that oil production will not increase before 1999 or 2000.
Oil output fell two percent to 6.03 million barrels per day last year.
The 6.03 million barrels per day output is the lowest level in three decades.
The percentage drop in output was the smallest since 1987.
Oil output from Russia fell to an average of 5.60 million barrels per day in the first two months of this year.
The first two months of 2023 output is two percent lower than the same period last year.
Some producers estimate that total output could be halved by the year 2000 under current tax regimes.
Analysts believe that steep declines in production are likely over, but an upturn will be challenging.
Around 26 percent of Russia's 139,000 oil wells are not operational.

Ansett Australia is a loss-making airline.
Ansett Australia stated it would not survive without major changes.
Rod Eddington is the executive chairman of Ansett Australia.
Eddington indicated that Ansett needed to sell non-core assets to improve its financial situation.
Ansett aims to free up cash and improve operating performance.
Ansett plans to acquire eight new aircraft to rationalise its fleet.
The new aircraft orders are valued at over A$2 billion.
The competition for the new aircraft orders is between Airbus Industrie and Boeing Co.
Ansett is jointly owned by Air New Zealand and News Corp.
Eddington described Ansett as an excellent airline but a poor business.

Heavy late-March rains improved Ivorian mid-crop cocoa harvest prospects.
March rainfall totals reached long-term average levels after a February drought.
A National Weather centre spokesman stated that recent rains have been satisfactory.
Official weather data indicated that rains totaled 742 mm in the third 10 days of March.
The previous 10 days of March recorded 208 mm of rainfall.
An average of 111 mm of rain fell in March.
Weather data suggested that March rains were in line with a 20-year average of around 105 mm.
Rains were spread widely over Ivory Coast's cocoa belt, with heaviest falls in central areas.
Crop analysts indicated that the mid-crop pod-count will determine harvest volumes.
Predictions for the 1996/97 mid-crop could exceed 150,000 tonnes if rains are sufficient.

Chinese President Jiang Zemin met with future Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa in Beijing.
Jiang Zemin pledged support for Tung Chee-hwa during their meeting.
Jiang stated that Tung's appointment marks the dawn of a new era.
Tung Chee-hwa will lead Hong Kong after its return to Chinese rule on July 1 next year.
Tung is a shipping magnate and will be Hong Kong's first Chinese chief executive after over 150 years of British colonial rule.
Tung was formally appointed by Premier Li Peng on Monday prior to his meeting with Jiang.
Residents of Hong Kong are interested in Tung's plans for his post-colonial administration.
Tung has warned Hong Kong's people to be sensitive to China's sovereign rights.
A 400-member Selection Committee of Hong Kong residents officially chose Tung with an 80 percent majority.
Premier Li Peng congratulated Tung and described the appointment as an historic moment.

Hershey Foods Corp is the top U.S. producer of chocolate and other confections.
Hershey Foods Corp is looking to establish a presence in the cookie and sweet snack market.
The sweet snack category generates about $30 billion annually in U.S. sales.
Chocolate and other candy generate about $11 billion in annual U.S. sales.
Hershey will pursue acquisitions and develop products to enter the sweet snack market.
Hershey has launched the Reese's Crunchy Cookie Peanut Butter Cup, which combines a chocolate cookie and a peanut butter cup.
William Christ stated there is a fine line between candy bars and cookies.
Hershey's dry pasta business remains profitable but faces challenges from high flour prices and price competition.
William Christ believes Hershey's dry pasta operations have the lowest costs in the United States.
Hershey acquired Leaf North America for $437 million in late 1996, enhancing its position in the U.S. candy market.

Tung Chee-hwa stated there will be no Tiananmen crackdowns in Hong Kong after China's takeover.
Martin Lee, leader of Hong Kong's Democratic Party, urged Tung to take action to support his words.
Tung made his vow on the U.S. ABC News 'Nightline' television program.
Tung promised to protect the right to protest in Hong Kong.
The British colony of Hong Kong reverts to China at midnight on June 30.
The Tiananmen massacre of 1989 is a significant memory for Hong Kong's population of 6.4 million.
Tung stated that the Tiananmen Square crackdown could not happen in Hong Kong.
Tung emphasized that demonstrations are part of Hong Kong's culture and life.
Lee expressed that Tung's comments contradicted his plans to curb civil rights.
China's parliament has declared Hong Kong's existing laws on public order and lawful assembly null and void after June 30.

Tyco International Ltd. made a $4 billion bid for American Standard Companies Inc.
American Standard rejected Tyco's offer and Tyco will not pursue a merger.
David Brownell is the Senior Vice President of Tyco.
Tyco has not engaged in hostile takeovers historically.
Tyco had no further contact with American Standard after the offer was rejected.
Tyco's offer was $50 a share, totaling about $4 billion.
American Standard became a public company in February 1995.
American Standard's board of directors concluded that remaining independent was in the best interest of its shareholders.
American Standard's stock price has doubled since it went public in 1995.
American Standard plans to proceed with a secondary public offering and share repurchase next month.

Netscape Communications Corp. is pursuing legal action against Microsoft Corp.
Analysts believe this legal action may reduce investor enthusiasm for both companies' stocks.
Gary Reback is Netscape's outside counsel at Wilson Sonsini Goodrich and Rosati.
Reback has urged the Department of Justice to take action against Microsoft for alleged violations.
Tim O'Reilly is the head of O'Reilly & Associates.
A Justice Department official recently approached O'Reilly regarding Microsoft's behavior.
Microsoft has denied the allegations made by Netscape.
Brad Chase is the vice president of marketing for Microsoft's Internet division.
Chase accused Netscape of not supporting open Internet standards.
Analysts noted that legal uncertainty could negatively impact the companies' stock performance.

Talks between South Korea and China have not resolved the situation of a senior North Korean defector in Beijing.
The defector, Hwang Jang-yop, has been in Seoul's mission in Beijing for eight days.
South Korean Foreign Ministry spokesman Lee Kyu-hyung stated that there has been no real progress in talks with China.
Lee denied a report from Japan's Yomiuri newspaper that Hwang could leave Beijing for asylum in South Korea this week.
China demanded a meeting with Hwang to confirm his desire to defect and a signed promise from South Korean President Kim Young-sam.
Lee stated that it is too early to discuss when Hwang could leave Beijing.
South Korean officials in Beijing indicated that talks with Chinese officials are ongoing.
Embassy spokesman Chang Moon Ik reported that no results have been achieved so far.
China insisted that Hwang's case be resolved through dialogue between South and North Korea.
A South Korean official stated that it is impossible to resolve the defection issue through direct talks with North Korea.

An advisor to Governor Chris Patten's inner cabinet stated that property in Hong Kong has become highly sought after.
Chen Kwan-yiu is a member of the executive council.
Chen Kwan-yiu indicated that a quick solution to Hong Kong's property issues is unlikely.
Chen Kwan-yiu claimed that the current supply of flats is adequate for demand.
Chen Kwan-yiu compared property in Hong Kong to gold in the 1960s, suggesting it is kept as an investment.
Chen Kwan-yiu stated that this has led to abnormal demand for property.
The economist suggested that providing more land for residential use could solve the property problem.
Hong Kong's property sector has faced criticism for rising housing prices.
Many young working adults in Hong Kong live with their parents due to high rents.
Retiree Alex Lo expressed that young people in Hong Kong struggle to own homes.

Brandon Tartikoff was named chairman of the board of Greenhouse Networks.
Greenhouse Networks is an original content developer for America Online Inc.
The appointment is part of an initiative to create specialized online networks.
America Online's stock increased by more than 11 percent to $47.
America Online announced it was acquiring LightSpeed Media Inc.
LightSpeed Media Inc. is known for producing Internet soap operas and shows.
Greenhouse Networks plans to develop an interactive entertainment network for AOL and the Internet.
The entertainment network will be based in Los Angeles.
Tartikoff previously served as president of NBC Entertainment from 1980 to 1991.
Tartikoff's first project with Greenhouse and AOL will be called 'Begg'.

H. Wayne Huizenga continued to acquire new car franchises.
Tom Webb is the chief economist of the National Automobile Dealers Association (NADA).
Webb stated that traditional dealers are expected to capture more of the used vehicle market.
Webb expressed a favorable outlook for the automobile industry during a news conference.
Republic Industries Inc. announced the purchase of Wallace Automotive Group.
Wallace Automotive Group operates Ford, Nissan, Dodge, Mitsubishi, and two Lincoln-Mercury dealerships in southeast Florida.
The purchase of Wallace Automotive Group was valued at $55 million.
Republic's total new dealer revenue estimates for 1997 are about $2.8 billion.
Republic is now the largest new vehicle dealer group in the country in terms of revenues.
Webb stated that economies of scale benefits stop after selling 100 vehicles a month.

Kenneth Dam is the chairman of a National Research Council report on computer encoding technology.
Dam stated that the report's findings from a year ago are still valid.
Dam is a law professor at the University of Chicago.
Dam told Reuters that a government access approach favored by the Clinton administration is not ready for widespread use.
Encryption is important for online commerce and global communications on the Internet.
Encryption scrambles information and makes it unreadable without a password or software key.
The Clinton administration bars the export of strong encryption unless it includes a key recovery feature.
Key recovery allows the government to decode messages by accessing software keys.
Critics argue that poorly designed key recovery systems could create vulnerabilities for hackers.
Dam echoed the NRC report's findings that key recovery is not sufficiently reliable yet.

Nicola Horlick announced her resignation from Deutsche Morgan Grenfell (DMG) on Thursday.
Horlick described a feeling of turmoil among fund managers at DMG following her resignation.
A spokesman for Horlick stated she planned to take legal action against DMG for constructive dismissal.
Horlick had been suspended pending an internal investigation into a potential breach of her contract.
The dispute involved allegations that Horlick intended to leave and take staff with her.
Last year, MGAM faced a scandal over misvaluations in three of its funds.
Peter Young was sacked from MGAM following the misvaluation scandal.
Horlick's suspension caused unease among large pension fund clients at DMG.
Horlick received a promotion to managing director shortly before her suspension.
Deutsche Bank agreed to a compensation package of around 200 million pounds to address investor losses.

Chinese police have detained dissident Wang Donghai.
Amnesty International has accused the Chinese government of torturing, imprisoning, and killing those who speak out.
Wang's family was informed by police in Hangzhou that he would be sent to a 'study class'.
The term 'study class' is a euphemism for coercive ideological reform.
Two public security officers took Wang away but did not provide a reason for his detention.
Wang's family was not allowed to meet him or know his location.
Wang's sister suspects his detention is related to fellow dissident Chen Longde.
Chen Longde jumped from a third-floor window on August 17 due to mistreatment by a prison official.
Wang and Chen Longde were ordered to serve one year and three years of 're-education through labour', respectively.
Wang was previously jailed for two years for organizing protests after the Tiananmen Square crackdown in 1989.

Harnischfeger Industries Inc is led by chief executive officer Jeffery Glade.
Jeffery Glade believes acquiring Giddings & Lewis Inc is the best option for Harnischfeger.
Giddings & Lewis Inc is based in Fond Du Lac, Wisconsin.
Harnischfeger has made a $747 million unsolicited tender offer for Giddings.
Harnischfeger is seeking other acquisitions regardless of the outcome of the Giddings offer.
Jeffery Glade stated that this is not Harnischfeger's last acquisition in the industrial product service group.
The machine tool and material handling industry is estimated to be worth more than $80 billion.
Jeffery Glade described the industry as poorly served and fragmented.
Giddings is a supplier of industrial automation products and machine tools.
Giddings' board of directors issued a rejection to Harnischfeger's offer, requesting a two-year 'stand still' agreement.

Automakers plan to introduce new sport/utility vehicle models at the North American International Auto Show.
The auto show takes place in Detroit and showcases advancements in size, style, luxury, and refinement of vehicles.
Analysts are particularly interested in Ford Motor Co.'s Lincoln Navigator and Chrysler Corp.'s Dodge Durango.
The Dodge Durango features styling elements from the Dodge Dakota pickup truck.
Subaru is introducing the Forester, a car-based hybrid sport/utility vehicle.
U.S. compact sport/utility vehicle sales grew by 17.9 percent in 1996, totaling 1,575,627 units.
Compact sport/utility vehicles accounted for 11.3 percent of the market in 1996.
Full-size sport/utility vehicles experienced a growth of 51.5 percent in 1996, totaling 379,260 vehicles.
In 1996, trucks, including sport/utility vehicles and minivans, made up 66 percent of Chrysler's total vehicle sales.
Ford's Navigator is based on the F-150 pickup truck and is expected to be priced in the mid-$40,000 range.

Novell Inc outlined a five-year game plan to reduce dependence on its network operating system business.
The plan aims to diversify Novell's revenue base into faster-growing software businesses.
Joseph Marengi is the president and chief operating officer of Novell Inc.
Novell is considering using its $1 billion in cash for selective technology acquisitions.
Marengi stated that Novell's strategy is focused on building its business as a standalone company.
Novell has a market capitalization of $4 billion, $1 billion in cash, and $1.5 billion in revenues.
Marengi indicated that Novell's core NetWare operating systems business is expected to decline to 40 percent of total revenues.
By 2002, Novell expects to generate 25 percent of its revenues from platform-independent products and 25 percent from network applications software.
Novell's strategy includes moving beyond its dominance in the client/server-based local area network market.
Marengi believes Novell will displace Microsoft Corp's Exchange product as the number two electronic messaging product in the world.

Share markets in and around China are sensitive to the health of Deng Xiaoping.
Analysts stated that the issue regarding Deng's health is now emotional and has little economic significance.
Most stock markets in the China region gained ground on Wednesday after losses on Tuesday due to rumors about Deng's health.
Beijing reported that there had been no major change in Deng's condition.
An executive from a major Chinese brokerage stated that Deng's health is the top political concern for Chinese stock markets.
The markets are expected to fluctuate sharply leading up to Deng's death.
Few investors in Chinese stock markets expect Deng's death to cause long-term social instability.
Investors are concerned about a short-term power struggle that could negatively affect stock markets.
Foreign brokers in Shanghai view the impact of Deng's health as temporary and diminishing over time.
Analysts in Taiwan believe that the effect of Deng's death on the markets will depend on the performance of Taiwan's markets at that time.

Statistics Canada admitted to making a significant error in calculating the depth of Canada's unemployment problem.
The monthly payroll report was scheduled to be released on Thursday.
Statistics Canada announced it will delay the payroll report until May 6 to correct its methods.
The delay is intended to fix inflated figures from December and January.
Peter Lys is the director of Statistics Canada's labor division.
Peter Lys stated that an error was discovered during the review of the February numbers.
Peter Lys did not disclose how inflated the job creation figures for December and January were.
The most recent payroll report indicated that 9,000 new employees were added in January and 134,000 in December.
The error occurred while Statistics Canada was fine-tuning its methodology for the survey.
Canada's unemployment rate was reported at 9.3 percent in March, down from 9.7 percent in February.

The king is dead, long live the king.
Chinese President Jiang Zemin has been designated to succeed paramount leader Deng Xiaoping for seven years.
Deng Xiaoping died last week at the age of 92 in Beijing.
Analysts claim Jiang Zemin has acted quickly to establish his own legacy since Deng's death.
Western diplomats have observed signals indicating Jiang's attempts to distance himself from Deng.
Chinese political analysts warn that Jiang is competing against powerful rivals who may not play fair.
One political analyst stated that Jiang Zemin is not a strong leader like Mao Zedong or Deng Xiaoping.
On the second day of official mourning for Deng, Jiang vowed to achieve greater successes than Deng's reforms.
A political analyst criticized Jiang for making premature statements that could be used against him.
Jiang Zemin faces challenges from leftist hardliners and other political aspirants as he navigates his leadership.

British supermarket group Safeway Plc is currently experiencing a zero inflation rate excluding petrol.
Deputy chairman David Webster stated that inflation excluding petrol is probably zero.
Webster claimed that the fall in prices is not related to a price war.
Webster expressed that shoppers are tightening their budgets more than usual.
Webster described the situation as a sector issue.
Webster believes that a price war is very unlikely.
Safeway reported that price inflation fell from a modest 1.1 percent gain in the five weeks to January 4.
Safeway's sales growth during the key Christmas trading period was 5.2 percent.
Sales growth over the first 16 weeks of the second half slowed to a 4.5 percent gain.
Webster noted that both the sector and Safeway have seen a sharp decline in overall sales performance in the last four weeks.

Czech Industry and Trade Minister Vladimir Dlouhy stated that a devaluation of the crown might be needed if the current account deficit does not decrease by the end of next year.
Dlouhy mentioned that a devaluation is not currently necessary to boost exports or address the current account deficit, which is forecasted at 5 to 6 percent of gross domestic product this year.
During a panel discussion, Dlouhy indicated that if the current account deficit continues to grow, a devaluation might be considered around the turn of 1997-98.
Some independent economists have suggested that a nominal devaluation of the currency may be necessary if the trade deficit does not decrease.
The government and other economists believe that net capital inflow, along with tourism and services revenue, can cover the merchandise trade deficit.
The merchandise trade deficit grew to 85.3 billion crowns in the first seven months of 1996, compared to a 49.5 billion crown deficit during the same period the previous year.
Dlouhy expressed a desire to see stabilization of the deficit increase during the first half of next year.
Dlouhy stated that if the deficit remains around five percent of GDP, the economy can finance it with revenue from tourism and services.
Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus and central bank governor Josef Tosovsky have both ruled out a devaluation of the crown.
Dlouhy is opposed to protectionist measures and prefers to use legislative tools like the anti-dumping law and stricter quality controls to improve the trade balance.

Colombian union leaders representing 800,000 state workers launched a nationwide strike on Tuesday.
The impact of the strike on vital economic sectors was not immediately clear apart from disruption in public transport.
Labor leaders claimed the strike would disrupt air traffic, oil production, telecommunications, and non-emergency health services.
Early morning reports indicated that, apart from shortages of public transportation, everything appeared to be running at or close to normal.
A bus was torched outside the central city of Ibague, but there were no immediate reports of violence or serious vandalism.
President Ernesto Samper warned of 'the dark forces of chaos' in a national address on Monday night.
Ismael Enrique Arenas, a senior official with Ecopetrol, stated there was no immediate effect on exploration or production activity.
Private oil companies working under contracts with Ecopetrol were also unaffected by the strike.
Francisco Hernandez, a spokesman for El Dorado international airport, reported that operations were 'more or less normal' early Tuesday.
Some airlines, including Continental Airlines Inc and AMR Corp's American Airlines, suspended operations in and out of Colombia as a security precaution.

United News & Media Plc reported a 12 percent profit increase in its first year after a merger.
The merger effectively doubled the size of United News & Media Plc.
United News, publisher of The Express and Daily Star, merged with MAI in a three billion pound deal.
The company's profit before tax and exceptional items for 1996 was 290.2 million pounds.
Earnings per share increased by 15 percent to 40 pence.
Chief executive Clive Hollick stated that the company met expectations set during the merger.
The profit figure exceeded most analysts' forecasts.
United shares increased by 9.5 pence to 750 by 1130 GMT.
The company expects annual savings of 43 million pounds by 1998 due to the merger and restructuring.
United spent over 750 million pounds on acquisitions last year and recouped around 300 million from disposals.

Seven Network Ltd reported a 31.5 percent fall in net profit for the half year to December 31.
The net profit fell to A$62.98 million from A$91.88 million a year earlier after paying A$34.3 million in tax.
Gary Rice is the managing director of Seven Network Ltd.
Gary Rice expects a slightly better performance in the second half of the 1996/97 year compared to the same period a year earlier.
Seven Network Ltd is about 20 percent owned by chairman Kerry Stokes.
Analysts forecast Seven to report a net profit before abnormals of A$59 million to A$65 million for the first half.
Seven's shares declined despite the overall market hitting a record high.
Seven Network Ltd is also 15 percent owned by News Corp Ltd.
Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer (MGM) reported earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) of US$16.7 million for the period from October 10 last year to December 31.
Seven declared a half year dividend of 4.5 cents, steady with the same period in 1995/96.

3Com Corp. stock lost more than a quarter of its value on Monday.
3Com announced that its fiscal third-quarter earnings will be less than Wall Street expected.
3Com is the second largest networking vendor in the United States.
3Com cut prices of its ethernet network products due to rising competition from Intel Corp.
43 percent of 3Com's revenue comes from ethernet network products.
3Com's stock fell $13.50 to $37.25 in Nasdaq trading.
More than 36 million shares of 3Com were traded, making it the most active stock in U.S. markets.
3Com expects to report earnings per share in the range of mid-40s to low 50 cents for the quarter ending February 28.
Wall Street expected 3Com to earn 60 cents per share according to First Call.
3Com's third-quarter revenues are projected to reach $770 million to $810 million, missing analyst forecasts by at least $20 million.

Deng Xiaoping died at the age of 92.
A eulogy for Deng was broadcast live from Beijing's Great Hall of the People.
The eulogy was shown on a giant screen in Shanghai's People's Square.
Hundreds of people gathered in Shanghai to watch the tribute.
President Jiang Zemin delivered a tribute to Deng Xiaoping.
Funereal music was played from speakers near the screen.
Gu Qi, a 65-year-old resident, expressed gratitude for Deng's contributions to China.
Gu Qi has lived in his apartment for over 30 years.
Official mourning began at 10:00 a.m. with sirens sounding nationwide.
Trading on Shanghai's stock exchange continued, but volumes dropped significantly.

The French government halted the sale of Thomson SA to Lagardere Groupe.
The French government aims to privatise Thomson SA to create a large French defence company.
Thomson's 58-percent owned subsidiary is Thomson-CSF.
French defence firms face shrinking defence budgets and industry restructuring in Europe.
President Jacques Chirac announced plans for Aerospatiale to merge with Dassault Aviation.
Chirac expressed a desire for strong French defence groups to compete in Europe.
Most of Germany's defence activities are controlled by Daimler-Benz AG.
Britain has two major defence companies: British Aerospace Plc and General Electric Co Plc.
The French government preferred Lagardere's offer for Thomson over Alcatel Alsthom's offer.
The government was concerned that French interests would lose control in an alliance with Alcatel.

Coles Myer Ltd reported a 41 percent increase in half-year earnings.
This is Coles' first profit rise in almost two years.
The result improved Coles' share price despite a weaker market.
Coles experienced two years of declining profits and consumer spending issues.
Coles reported a net profit of A$273.6 million for the half-year ended January 26.
This net profit is an increase from A$194.5 million a year ago.
Before abnormals, net earnings increased 23 percent to A$229 million.
Coles' shares rose 10 cents to A$6.01 (US$4.74) in morning trade.
A broker stated that expectations of a turnaround are influencing the stock price.
Coles provided a positive forecast for the full year ending July 27, expecting more double-digit profit growth.

Ivory Coast's mid-crop cocoa harvest is projected to exceed 100,000 tonnes.
Rains may increase production to 160,000 tonnes or more, according to crop analysts.
One analyst stated that there is currently about two-thirds of the estimated 160,000 tonnes on trees.
The total harvest depends on weather conditions over the next three weeks.
National weather centre forecasters predict that rains will strengthen in the next two to three weeks.
The analyst noted that there are fewer pods than last year, but the situation is not worse than the average of the past four to five years.
Ivory Coast recorded a total crop of 1.2 million tonnes in 1995/96 after a mid-crop of 200,000 tonnes.
Crop analysts have differing opinions on mid-crop data and five-year averages.
Main crop arrivals by March 7 totaled at least 920,000 tonnes, approaching last year's total of one million tonnes.
An exporter indicated that main crop cocoa is diminishing, but some remains at the farmer level in certain areas.

China expressed mixed feelings about the World Trade Organisation (WTO), acknowledging its importance while criticizing it for neglecting poorer nations.
Shen Guofang, a spokesman for China's Foreign Ministry, stated that a recent WTO meeting in Singapore did not adequately address the differing needs of member states.
Shen claimed that the outcomes of the meeting primarily reflected the interests of developed countries.
The China Daily newspaper reported that China's enthusiasm for joining the WTO was diminishing after years of unsuccessful efforts.
Wu Jiahuang, director general of the customs administration's tariffs department, was quoted as saying that China has become indifferent to WTO accession.
Wu compared China's attempts to join the WTO to a 'sunken boat' and an 'ailing tree'.
Western diplomats suggested that Wu's comments reflected internal disagreements about the global economy rather than a change in China's desire to join the WTO.
Shen clarified that the China Daily report did not necessarily represent Beijing's official stance on WTO membership.
China seeks to join the WTO under terms favorable to developing countries, but some members, particularly the United States, argue that China's economy is too strong for such treatment.
Wu indicated that China's leadership believes negotiations on entry terms with WTO members have been politically influenced.

Wm. Wrigley Jr Co is looking for ways to revitalize the domestic chewing gum market.
The domestic chewing gum market saw about a one percent drop in physical sales volume in 1996.
William Piet is the vice president of corporate affairs and corporate secretary at Wm. Wrigley Jr Co.
Piet stated that new advertising, merchandising, or improved products are needed for the category.
Piet cautioned that the decline in the overall domestic chewing gum market does not signal a disaster.
The chewing gum industry has been growing at an average annual rate of 2.5 percent.
Wrigley's chewing gum brands surpassed about a 50 percent market share at the end of 1996.
North America accounts for roughly 46 percent of Wrigley's business.
Wrigley will add Cambodia to the list of about 120 countries where it sells products.
Wrigley plans to begin construction for a new factory in Russia, expected to be operational in early 1999.

The board of utilities group Lyonnaise des Eaux was scheduled to meet on Wednesday afternoon to approve the 1996 accounts.
Lyonnaise des Eaux is involved in merger talks with holding company Cie de Suez.
The merger could provide assets of Cie de Suez to Lyonnaise des Eaux.
Lyonnaise des Eaux is expected to publish its results on Thursday morning.
Analysts expect Lyonnaise des Eaux to show a net attributable profit of between 1.0 and 1.5 billion francs for 1996.
Lyonnaise des Eaux reported a profit of 906 million francs in 1995.
The market is seeking details about the merger, including financial terms and industrial strategy.
Suez owns a 16.8 percent stake in Lyonnaise des Eaux.
Suez's subsidiary Tractebel will remain independent in Belgium as part of the merger discussions.
Analysts have expressed skepticism about the industrial rationale behind the merger.

The bidding war for Conrail Inc. is nearing its conclusion.
Legal and regulatory battles are expected to follow the bidding war.
CSX Corp. and Norfolk Southern Corp. are the rival bidders for Conrail.
CSX raised its offer for Conrail to provide shareholders with an additional $870 million.
The revised deal from CSX is valued at $9.3 billion, or approximately $102 per Conrail share.
Norfolk Southern increased its all-cash offer to about $10.5 billion, or $115 per share.
Conrail believes that a merger with CSX is a better strategic fit than with Norfolk Southern.
Norfolk Southern is challenging a provision that prevents CSX or Conrail from seeking another merger partner until 1999.
A hearing regarding the exclusivity provision is scheduled for January 9 in Philadelphia.
Norfolk Southern previously lost a court challenge regarding the exclusivity provision.

Netscape Communications Corp will present a vision for future product use on Monday.
The vision includes coordinating activities between companies and their customers, partners, suppliers, and distributors.
The market for secured interconnections between companies using Internet technology is expected to grow significantly.
Internet analysts and investors anticipate that electronic commerce will exceed previous projections for merchandising and advertising growth.
The market for Extranets could be larger than the projected $10 billion growth of the Intranet software market by the year 2000.
Marc Andreessen is the co-founder and senior vice president of technology at Netscape.
Andreessen has discussed the potential market for Extranets since the middle of last year.
Extranets are described as external networks of interlinked corporate Intranets.
Netscape's software allows companies to provide partners with access to parts of their Intranet.
Netscape plans to release next-generation products, including client software called Mercury and server products codenamed Apollo, in early 1998.

Shi Xin played Deng Xiaoping in the movie 'Battles for Glory over Taihang Mountains'.
The movie premiered in December.
Shi Xin has been offered roles as Deng Xiaoping in five other films since the premiere.
Shi Xin expressed a desire to avoid being typecast in the role of Deng Xiaoping.
Deng Xiaoping died at the age of 92.
Deng Xiaoping's death occurred on Shi Xin's 25th birthday.
Shi Xin found it challenging to portray Deng Xiaoping due to the character's significance.
Shi Xin lost weight for the role by eating mostly tomatoes and cucumbers.
Shi Xin studied books and photo albums to prepare for the role of Deng Xiaoping.
The movie 'Battles for Glory' did not recoup its production costs.

Tung Chee-hwa plans to ban foreign donations to political groups in Hong Kong.
Tung Chee-hwa was criticized for donating money to Britain's Conservative Party.
Critics accused Tung Chee-hwa of being a hypocrite and having double standards.
Tung Chee-hwa's credibility as Hong Kong's leader is considered at stake.
Tung Chee-hwa donated 50,000 sterling (US$81,500) to the Conservative Party before Britain's April 1992 general election.
Tung Chee-hwa's donation was confirmed by his office and reported in the South China Morning Post.
Tung Chee-hwa stated he made modest donations to the Conservative Party in the past.
A Tung aide said the donation was made in a personal capacity when he was chairman of Orient Overseas (International) Ltd.
Tung Chee-hwa resigned from his position at Orient Overseas to run for leader after Governor Chris Patten's departure.
Martin Lee, leader of the Democratic Party, met with United States President Bill Clinton at the White House.

Dalgety Plc posted a profit of 43 million pounds ($70.5 million) for the six months ending December 31, 1996.
Dalgety Plc experienced an 8.5 percent fall in profits compared to the previous period.
Sales of beef and animal feeds at Dalgety Plc declined.
Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) in cattle is known as mad-cow disease.
The European Union imposed a worldwide ban on British beef exports in March 1996.
The culling of thousands of British cattle has been delayed.
Dalgety chief executive Richard Clothier expressed optimism about future performance improvements.
Analysts forecasted pre-tax profits for Dalgety Plc to be between 41 and 45.5 million pounds.
Dalgety maintained its dividend at 8.5p.
Dalgety shares increased by 2p to 341p in early trade.

The Explorer from Ford Motor Co. is expected to offer sales incentives for the first time.
The Explorer has been the best-selling four-door vehicle in the United States for nearly two years.
The Explorer is facing increased competition since its introduction six years ago.
The new Expedition full-sized sport utility from Ford is expected to compete with the Explorer.
Chrysler Corp. Cherokees are available for as little as $199 a month due to subsidized leases.
Wesley Brown, director of global product analysis at CSM Forecasting, predicts a national program for the Explorer by the end of the year.
Analyst Jack Kirnan from Salomon Brothers predicts Ford will launch lease incentives for the Explorer in the next 60 days.
Kirnan believes the new Expedition will cannibalize sales from the Explorer, prompting Ford to implement incentives.
Ford executives estimate the Expedition will take 10 percent to 15 percent of the Explorer's sales.
Explorer sales have declined for five consecutive months, with August sales reported at 27,615, down 10.7 percent.

The number of banks charging non-customers for using their automated teller machines doubled over the past six months.
About 45 percent of ATMs added a surcharge for non-customers, up from 23 percent in October.
The average fee for using an ATM increased by 20 percent to $1.15 from 96 cents.
Edmund Mierzwinski is the programme director for the U.S. Public Interest Research Group.
Connecticut and Iowa have banned the practice of charging non-customers for ATM use.
Twelve other states and the federal government are considering legislation against ATM surcharges.
The two largest ATM networks, Visa's Plus and Mastercard's Cirrus, lifted a prohibition on surcharges one year ago.
Banks defended the surcharge practice by stating it helps pay for ATMs in new locations.
The American Bankers Association stated that the marketplace should decide ATM prices.
Among the 300 largest banks, 53 percent of ATMs charged a fee, compared to 40 percent of smaller bank ATMs and 6 percent of credit union ATMs.

Morgan Grenfell and former fund manager Nicola Horlick are in a dispute.
Pension fund clients are reassessing their relationships with Morgan Grenfell.
Nicola Horlick resigned from her position after being suspended for an alleged breach of contract.
Horlick is in meetings with legal representatives in London.
Horlick's lawyers stated she seeks an amicable settlement with Morgan Grenfell.
Horlick is prepared to sue if a settlement cannot be reached.
John Farr, a partner at Herbert Smith, mentioned Horlick is hopeful for an amicable resolution.
Details regarding the reasons for Horlick's departure from MGAM are not fully disclosed.
MGAM has initiated a damage-limitation campaign by contacting clients and holding meetings.
The London Borough of Lewisham and Norfolk County Council expressed concerns about recent developments at MGAM.

Papua New Guinea's Australian-listed stocks fell five to ten percent on Monday.
International investors reacted to the army's attempt to force the PNG government aside.
Orogen Minerals Ltd, which is 51 percent owned by the PNG government, fell seven percent to A$3.20.
Other stocks dropped as much as ten percent during afternoon trade.
The head of the army and the police commissioner told Prime Minister Julius Chan to resign or be forced aside in two days.
The army and police are unhappy with the government's employment of mercenaries to subdue secessionists on Bougainville Island.
Brokers and analysts expressed concerns about a potential army mutiny and civil unrest in Port Moresby spreading to remote areas.
Michael Heffernan, a research director at Shaw Stockbroking, warned that local tribes might disrupt mining operations.
Major mining projects in Papua New Guinea often face disputes with local tribal groups.
The Bougainville Copper mine was shut down in 1989 due to landowner sabotage and a revolt.

Case Corp plans to spend $950 million in the next four years to revamp its product line.
Jean-Pierre Rosso is the chief executive of Case Corp, which is based in Racine, Wisconsin.
Case Corp aims to replace all major agricultural products by the end of the century.
Many construction products will also be revamped as part of the overhaul.
A new tractor series, the MX Series, will enter production in the spring.
The MX Series tractors range from 85 to 115 horsepower and represent about 30 percent of tractor sales worldwide for Case.
Orders for the MX Series tractors in the United States and Europe have exceeded company plans.
The MX Series tractors will be produced in Racine and the United Kingdom.
The switch from the German production site is expected to lower costs due to labor and logistics.
The new tractor design utilizes more common components to reduce costs.

General Motors Corp. stock rose on Friday due to optimism about a potential dividend increase and stock buyback programme.
Analysts expect GM's board of directors to announce a stock buyback programme of up to $5 billion.
GM shares increased by $1.125 to $63 after reaching a 52-week high of $63.75 on the New York Stock Exchange.
GM recently sold its Hughes Aircraft defence operations to Raytheon Corp. for $9.5 billion.
Analysts believe GM is trying to catch up with Chrysler Corp. and Ford Motor Co. in returning cash to shareholders.
CS First Boston analyst Nicholas Colas stated that it is time for GM to reward shareholders for their patience.
GM spokeswoman Toni Simonetti confirmed that the board would consider the dividend but did not comment on potential increases or buybacks.
Analysts estimated that GM's board will increase the quarterly dividend by 10 to 20 cents per share.
GM currently pays a quarterly dividend of 40 cents per share.
Analysts noted that GM ended 1996 with $15 billion in cash, which is $3 billion above its target.

NCR Corp. unveiled a prototype for a do-it-yourself retail checkout system on Friday.
The system is designed to speed supermarket checkout times and reduce shopper frustration.
The automated checkout system allows shoppers to scan, bag, and pay for groceries without cashier assistance.
NCR plans to introduce the self-checkout system in 1998 after in-store consumer testing this year.
NCR estimates there are more than 175,000 food store checkout lanes in the United States.
About 30 percent of those lanes are operated as cashier-assisted express lanes.
Joanne Walter, NCR's vice president of future retailing systems, stated the system targets frequent shoppers with a few items.
The initial system is aimed at food store express lanes, with future versions targeting other retail environments.
Walter mentioned that 65 percent of all retail purchases involve 20 items or less.
The automated checkout system is known as SCOT, which stands for Self Checkout Terminal.

China's domestic A share markets are expected to rise strongly in 1997 due to an improving national economy.
Analysts state that the market dynamics of 1996 will not be repeated as Beijing insists on steady development.
A recent crackdown on rampant share speculation has made the markets more cautious.
There is still significant capital in China seeking investment in the stock markets of Shanghai and Shenzhen.
Bank deposits in China are increasing at approximately 30 percent per year.
The Chinese government has restricted many other investment channels in recent months.
The government plans to introduce new scrip to the share markets to avoid volatility similar to that of 1996.
Company results for 1996 are anticipated to improve significantly compared to 1995 due to the recovering economy and interest rate cuts.
Shanghai's A share index reached a high of 1,313.917 points on December 12, 1996, while Shenzhen's A share index hit 502.77 points on the same day.
Analysts believe that share prices will not experience the same dramatic movements in 1997 as they did in 1996.

The Czech government expects the country's gross domestic product (GDP) to grow 5.4 percent in 1997.
The expected GDP growth for 1996 is 5.1 percent.
Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus announced these expectations after a cabinet session discussing the 1997 budget proposal.
The new budget is based on an annual average inflation forecast of 8.6 percent for 1997.
The revised inflation forecast for 1996 is 9.0 percent.
The country's current account deficit could reach 5.8 percent of GDP in 1997.
The projected current account deficit for 1996 is 5.7 percent of GDP.
The current account gap is expected to climb to about 150 billion crowns ($5.69 billion) in 1996.
The budget planned by the government is the fifth straight balanced budget, with spending and revenues at 549.1 billion crowns.
The cabinet proposes cutting personal income taxes by raising the threshold for taxable income to 28,800 crowns from 26,400 crowns.

China's President Jiang Zemin spoke publicly for the first time since the death of Deng Xiaoping.
Jiang Zemin vowed to push forward the reforms launched by Deng Xiaoping 18 years ago.
Jiang stated that the Communist Party of China, the Chinese army, and various ethnic groups are determined to turn grief into strength.
Jiang made these statements while speaking to Kazakhstan President Nursultan Nazarbayev.
Deng Xiaoping died at the age of 92 on Wednesday.
Jiang pledged to uphold Deng's theory to build socialism with Chinese characteristics.
Jiang stated that China would pursue Deng's reforms and opening up confidently.
Jiang described Deng's death as an immeasurable loss to the Party, army, and people of China.
Jiang holds the positions of Communist Party chief and head of the armed forces.
Analysts suggest that Jiang may face a power struggle with other potential leaders in the ruling party.

British supermarket group J. Sainsbury Plc issued a profits warning on Friday.
Sainsbury's shares fell by 13 percent following the profits warning.
Sainsbury projected pretax profits for the current year to be between 640 million and 650 million pounds.
The projected profits are below consensus forecasts of over 700 million pounds.
Sainsbury reported a 4.4 percent increase in sales from existing supermarket stores in the eight weeks to January 11.
The sales increase of 4.4 percent is an improvement from a three percent gain in October.
Tesco reported a 7.5 percent sales increase, which is higher than Sainsbury's increase.
Sainsbury's shares fell to 339 pence, dropping below Tesco's share price for the first time.
ASDA's shares decreased by 2.75 pence to 121.5 pence, and Safeway's shares dropped by 13 pence to 389.5 pence.
Analysts downgraded Sainsbury's profit forecasts for 1997/98.

Jan Sverak is a 31-year-old director who wears 'John Lennon' glasses.
Zdenek Sverak is a grey-bearded screenwriter and star.
Jan and Zdenek Sverak are a father and son team in the film industry.
They have become known for their storytelling of Czech post-communist nostalgia.
They received their second Oscar nomination for best foreign language feature for the film 'Kolya'.
'Kolya' tells the story of an ageing bachelor who takes in an abandoned Russian boy.
'Kolya' is set during the eve of Prague's 1989 'Velvet Revolution'.
The film 'Kolya' won a Golden Globe in January.
Critics consider 'Kolya' one of the best offerings from the region since the Czech new wave of the 1960s.
The Sverak team received their first Oscar nomination in 1992 for the film 'Elementary School'.

Pools of blood stain a dirt track in Uraba, a central region of Colombia.
The bodies of two slain workers are transported to the morgue in a truck.
Heavily armed police search for the killers in the banana plantations.
For the last decade, the banana industry in Uraba has been associated with violence.
Rightwing paramilitaries and leftist guerrillas compete for the allegiance of the local population.
The banana industry has influenced politics, the economy, and society in four municipalities of Colombia's 'banana belt' for 30 years.
Gloria Cuartas is the mayor of Apartado and has commented on the suffering behind banana production.
In the past, banana workers' unions were linked to guerrilla groups like the Maoist People's Liberation Army (EPL) and FARC.
Most EPL fighters disarmed in 1991 and formed a political movement called Esperanza, Paz y Libertad.
Esperanza, Paz y Libertad now controls the union Sintrainagro, representing 13,000 members.

Stericycle Inc is comfortable with Wall Street estimates of a break-even third quarter and a fourth-quarter operating profit.
Stericycle expects to have a profitable year for the first time in 1997.
Mark Miller, the chief executive of Stericycle, stated that the Dillon Read report predicts an operating profit in the fourth quarter of 1997.
Stericycle reported a loss of $2.4 million, or $0.30 per share, in 1996.
Mark Miller indicated that Stericycle would be close to moving into profitability in the first quarter of 1997.
Stericycle has been in business since 1989 and has never turned a profit.
Stericycle's stock has remained below its initial public offering price of $9 per share.
Stericycle's shares were unchanged at $8 on light trading volume.
Stericycle's 1997 revenues are projected to exceed $36 million.
Stericycle is the second-largest player in a $1 billion U.S. medical waste market.

Southcorp Holdings Ltd reported a 22.3 percent rise in first half net profit.
Southcorp's net profit after abnormals for the six months ended December 31, 1996, was A$64.92 million.
This net profit was an increase from A$52.36 million a year earlier.
Chief executive officer Graham Kraehe stated that Southcorp is on track to meet its year-end forecast.
Kraehe indicated that the year-end forecast is broadly in line with market expectations.
Market expectations for net profit before abnormals were around A$130 million.
Southcorp reported a net profit of A$124.22 million in 1995/96, including a record second half profit of A$64.3 million.
Kraehe mentioned that all three divisions showed profit improvement in the December 1996 half results.
The appliance division experienced the strongest growth despite lower sales.
Southcorp is building a manufacturing plant in Dalian, China, to make steel and aluminium cans.

Apple Computer Inc. is undertaking a second restructuring in a year.
Apple may announce bigger-than-expected job cuts and a significant loss for the second quarter.
Apple is expected to specify which product lines it plans to drop.
Apple announced in January that it expects to report quarterly losses until at least September 1997.
Speculation suggests Apple may need to fire between 2,000 and 5,000 of its 13,000 employees.
James Poyner, an analyst at Oppenheimer & Co, stated that layoffs could be deeper than original estimates.
Apple executives expect revenue for the fiscal year ending in September to decline about 20 percent to around $8 billion.
Apple stated it needs to cut at least $400 million in costs this year to break even.
Worldwide shipments of Macintosh computers are expected to fall to about 804,000 units in the March quarter.
Analysts speculate that Newton handheld computers could be discontinued or sold to another company.

One million tonnes of corn are rotting in storage in China's northern port of Dalian.
Traders predict that this will lead to tightened local supplies and increased prices before the new crop is available at year-end.
Up to 50 percent of the stored corn is unfit for milling, according to a trader in Hong Kong.
A trader in Hong Kong stated that prices for Dalian futures are expected to rise.
The new crop will not be available until January after farmers have dried it.
Traders indicated that if domestic prices continue to rise, exporting corn may not be viable.
A U.S. trader in Hong Kong mentioned that free on board (FOB) values in Dalian were 1,400 yuan ($168) per tonne for good quality corn.
Southern feed millers are rejecting Dalian corn based on quality, according to a regional trader.
The U.S. trader noted that in the U.S., low quality corn can be blended with high quality corn, but this is not possible in China.
China's recent demand for soymeal suggests a need for corn to mix with the protein product.

Philippe Jaffre is the chairman of French oil group Elf Aquitaine.
Jaffre is restructuring Elf Aquitaine to focus on its core oil and chemicals activities.
Elf Aquitaine was formerly a state-owned conglomerate.
Jaffre plans to give up control of the health and beauty products unit Sanofi.
Elf holds a 53 percent stake in Sanofi.
Sanofi has a promising product pipeline but requires funding to bring products to market.
Jean-Francois Dehecq is the chief executive of Sanofi.
Elf will not commit money to Sanofi's expansion but will allow it to seek alliances.
Elf Aquitaine is among the weakest performers in the oil industry.
In 1995, Elf's return on equity was 6.5 percent.

Bill Gates is the Chairman of Microsoft Corp.
Microsoft Corp. and Apple Computer Inc. have been longtime rivals.
Microsoft has become the largest independent producer of software for the Macintosh platform.
Apple is undergoing a reorganization to address losses and regain market share.
Bill Gates expressed interest in continuing to work with Apple.
Gates is confused by Apple's operating system strategy.
Microsoft has little need to worry about Apple.
About 80 percent of new desktop computers have Windows installed.
About 5 percent of new desktop computers have the Apple Macintosh operating system installed.
Java is gaining momentum and is supported by many companies.

Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko attended a mini-summit in Gabon with French-speaking African presidents.
The summit aimed to find a peaceful resolution to the war threatening Zaire's capital.
Mobutu wore a leopard skin cap during the summit.
Gabonese President Omar Bongo, who has been in power since 1967, greeted Mobutu at the summit.
The summit included the presidents of Chad, Congo, the Central African Republic, and Equatorial Guinea.
Cameroon's foreign minister represented Cameroon at the summit, which was chaired by the Organisation of African Unity (OAU).
The Zairean opposition newspaper Potentiel referred to the meeting as Mobutu's 'Goodbye summit.'
Zaire's Information Minister Kin-Kiey Mulumba stated that Mobutu would return to Zaire after the summit.
South Africa's President Nelson Mandela facilitated a meeting between Mobutu and rebel leader Laurent Kabila.
Hundreds of civilians and fighters were reported dead after a battle for Kenge, a town near Kinshasa.

China and the United States made progress in talks on a new textile accord on Thursday.
Negotiations could extend late into the night before a deadline for agreement.
Chief negotiator Rita Hayes stated that progress had been made on market access.
The talks aim to renew a 1994 textile accord and resolve a dispute over U.S. penalties on Chinese exports.
Washington could significantly cut China's textile quotas if an agreement is not reached before the January 31 deadline.
Rita Hayes indicated that there are still many issues to address, requiring a lot of work.
The Sino-U.S. textile pact was scheduled to expire on December 31 but was extended by one month.
Washington and Beijing are seeking to ease tensions over Chinese exports of textiles via third countries.
The United States has threatened multi-million dollar penalties over the issue.
China has threatened to retaliate by temporarily banning imports of some U.S. textiles, farm goods, and alcoholic drinks.

Breakfast cereal price wars are affecting the earnings of major cereal makers.
Kellogg Co. is expected to report flat earnings for the latest quarter.
Ralcorp Holdings Inc. is likely to report lower earnings.
Price cuts and promotions in the cereal business have negatively impacted Kellogg and Ralcorp.
Kellogg has lost sales to competitors like General Mills Inc.
General Mills' earnings rose 7.5 percent in its latest quarter due to increased market share from promotions.
Price cutting was initiated by Post Cereal, prompting other companies to follow.
Kellogg's market share decreased from 35 percent to about 33 percent.
Kellogg's domestic earnings are expected to decline due to lower sales and increased marketing spending.
Kellogg purchased Lender's Bagels from Kraft Foods Inc. for $455 million.

France will not allow Britain's General Electric Co Plc (GEC) to bid for the state's stake in Thomson-CSF for national security reasons.
GEC is in discussions with two French companies, Lagardere Groupe and Alcatel Alsthom, which are allowed to bid.
The Finance Ministry received offers for the 58 percent stake from Lagardere and Alcatel Alsthom, which is bidding with Dassault Industrie.
The French government has declared the proposals by Lagardere Groupe and Alcatel Alsthom and Dassault Industrie as admissible.
The proposal by GEC has not been admitted due to national security concerns regarding foreign ownership of more than 50 percent of Thomson-CSF.
GEC expressed regret over the rejection but stated it is in talks with Lagardere and Alcatel.
Analysts in London believe it was unlikely for GEC to win the tender over French companies.
Analysts suggest GEC might gain a stake by partnering with a French company.
GEC stated that the French government encouraged it to open talks with Lagardere and Alsthom.
Firm offers for Thomson-CSF are due by May 7, and the government aims to make a decision by the end of June.

Federal regulators and television broadcasters are working on a timetable for TV stations to provide high-definition digital broadcasts within 18 to 24 months.
The Federal Communications Commission plans to distribute free digital TV licenses to stations in the next two weeks.
The new digital service promises improved picture and sound quality.
The National Association of Broadcasters and the Association for Maximum Service Television proposed that 31 stations in the 10 largest metropolitan areas start broadcasting digital signals in 18 to 24 months.
In some markets, up to four stations would begin broadcasting in the proposed time frame.
The top 10 markets include New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, and Philadelphia.
Broadcasters previously indicated that they needed more time, estimating six years to install the necessary equipment for digital broadcasts.
Commissioner Susan Ness expressed support for the broadcasters' commitment to launching digital television.
FCC officials emphasized that key details regarding the number of digital broadcasts must be clarified.
FCC Chairman Reed Hundt proposed that major network-owned stations in the top 10 markets start providing digital signals within the next year.

Apple Computer Inc. is seeking outside investment in its Newton computer unit.
Apple is looking for new homes for at least a dozen technology projects it recently decided to stop funding.
The hand-held Newton computer unit was not closed during a restructuring last month.
Early versions of the Newton did not perform well four years ago.
Apple Chief Scientist Larry Tesler stated that the unit's latest offerings have received positive reviews.
Demand for the new eMate, a version of the Newton, is strong and costs around $800.
A small group of Apple executives is exploring alternatives for increasing investment in the Newton business.
Apple is cutting spending by an average of 25 percent across the company.
Apple plans to cut 4,100 jobs and take a $155 million restructuring charge in the second quarter ending March 31.
Tesler mentioned that Apple is looking for ways to keep discontinued work alive by licensing it to third parties.

Deng Xiaoping died at the age of 92 on Wednesday.
China's state television broadcasted images of Deng's body lying in state at Beijing's 301 Military Hospital.
Deng's body was draped with the hammer-and-sickle flag of Chinese communism and surrounded by flower petals.
Official mourning for Deng Xiaoping began after his death.
China Central Television dedicated its main evening newscast to scenes of farewell to Deng's body.
President Jiang Zemin, Deng's successor, led a group of mourners that included members of the Communist Party politburo.
Jiang Zemin shook hands with Deng's family but did not speak during the mourning.
Deng's body was carried in a glass-topped bier to Babaoshan cemetery for cremation.
Deng's wife, Zhuo Lin, and family members were shown visibly grieving during the broadcast.
People along the funeral cortege's route were shown crying and attaching white paper flowers of mourning to their jackets.

The Bank of China Group in Hong Kong and Macau (BOC) will not seek special treatment in Hong Kong after July 1.
Clarina Man is a deputy general manager in the bank's public relations division.
Clarina Man stated that BOC seeks no privileges after 1997 and does not intend to replace any bank in the territory.
Clarina Man mentioned that BOC will compete on a level-playing field in Hong Kong after July 1.
Hong Kong reverts to China at midnight on June 30.
The 1984 Sino-British treaty governing the handover pledged Hong Kong a considerable degree of self-rule and complete fiscal independence.
The 'one country, two systems' formula was espoused by China's late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.
Many Hong Kong people are concerned about potential cronyism and interference by Chinese officials and companies in Hong Kong affairs.
BOC is aware of concerns regarding the 'one country, two systems' formula and aims to observe it vigilantly.
BOC reported a year-on-year 20.5 percent rise in global pre-tax profit for the fiscal year ended December 31, 1996.

Guinness Plc assured investors that its joint ventures with LVMH are secure despite LVMH's decision to sell a third of its shares in Guinness.
Guinness finance director Phil Yea stated that the commercial arrangements with LVMH are unaffected by the share sale announcement.
Guinness and LVMH's Moet Hennessey operate approximately 15 joint ventures worldwide.
LVMH sold 135 million of its Guinness shares, representing about 7.0 percent of its holding, at a price of 414p per share.
The sale raised approximately 559 million pounds ($934.9 million) for LVMH.
Analysts suggested that the sale was influenced by rumors that LVMH needs funds to acquire the rest of DFS.
LVMH currently owns 58.75 percent of DFS.
One unnamed analyst commented that LVMH was dissatisfied with Guinness's trading statement and the company's share price performance.
LVMH plans to retain its remaining 14 percent stake in Guinness and continue developing business ties with the company.
Guinness purchased 2.3 percent of its shares that were released by the LVMH sale.

China expressed concern that its trade surplus with the United States might affect bilateral relations.
China released a White Paper defending its trade policies.
Vice Minister of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation Sun Zhenyu stated that China is taking steps to reduce the trade surplus.
Sun Zhenyu indicated that action is also needed from the U.S. government and American industry.
Sun Zhenyu noted that the trade surplus issue is a general concern for many Americans.
Sun Zhenyu suggested that failure to address the trade surplus could hinder economic and trade relations between China and the U.S.
Sun Zhenyu expressed hope that U.S. Vice President Al Gore's upcoming visit would help build mutual trust.
Sun Zhenyu mentioned the possibility of signing major contracts during the visit.
Sun Zhenyu stated that a deal for the sale of Boeing aircraft to China is a possibility, pending agreement on terms.
China's trade surplus with the United States rose to $3.72 billion in January, up from $2.74 billion in January of the previous year.

Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin will explain the Clinton administration's bank reform plan on Capitol Hill.
Lawmakers are expected to focus on what the Clinton plan omitted.
The Clinton proposal aims to eliminate the 1933 Glass-Steagall Act's separation of banking from other financial services.
The Clinton administration did not address the issue of allowing banks to combine with commercial firms.
Rubin announced two alternatives in the Clinton plan and left the decision to Congress.
Congress has been debating changes to U.S. banking laws for over a decade without success.
Opponents of mixing banking and commerce, led by Jim Leach, will question Rubin about the risks of unlimited mergers.
Proponents of mixing banking and commerce, including Marge Roukema and Richard Baker, will support the idea.
One alternative proposed by Rubin allows limited mixing of banking and commerce, excluding the largest nonfinancial firms.
The second alternative maintains the prohibition on mixing but keeps the exception for commercial firms owning savings and loan institutions.

Dresdner Bank and ABN AMRO Holding NV are interested in expanding their presence in the British fund management business.
Analysts have indicated that the acquisition options for these banks will be limited.
The price range for quoted asset management companies varies from around 125 million pounds to several billion pounds.
Top performers like Mercury Asset Management are considered prohibitively expensive.
Major players in the market have not indicated they are available for acquisition.
Weaker fund firms are not likely to attract interest from European banks seeking immediate market impact.
Some banks believe that the prices for asset management businesses are too high.
Insurance companies are also interested in acquiring more asset management business.
New entrants to the asset management field, including retailers and supermarkets, are expected to emerge.
Dresdner Bank announced a restructuring of its global fund management business to include non-German funds.

Australia's largest banks and insurance groups have paused their expansion plans for the past year while awaiting the Wallis report.
