The Financial System Inquiry was established in June last year by the Liberal/National government and chaired by Stan Wallis.
The Wallis report is scheduled to be released at noon on Wednesday.
Analysts expect Wallis to recommend easing restrictions on mergers between Australia's six largest financial groups.
National Australia Bank (NAB) is expected to pursue acquisitions of smaller banks like Westpac Banking Corp and ANZ Banking Group Ltd.
One bank announced a takeover of a smaller regional bank before the Wallis report was released.
Treasurer Peter Costello will not approve Westpac's plan to take over Bank of Melbourne until he reviews Wallis' recommendations.
Wallis is expected to ease rules on foreign takeovers of Australia's largest banks and reform prudential supervision systems.
Craig Drummond, head of research at J.B. Were, stated that the expectation is for Wallis to lead to an easing of merger rules.
The 'Six Pillars' policy, instituted by Labor Treasurer Paul Keating in 1990, prevents mergers among Australia's big four banks and two largest insurance groups.

Several days before a report on the Busang gold controversy, Freeport McMoRan Copper & Gold Inc. confirmed it had not found significant gold at the site in Indonesia.
Freeport reported finding 'insignificant amounts' of gold from preliminary tests of Busang last month.
Freeport has continued testing its original seven drill cores taken from the Busang site.
Freeport spokesman Kristin Lemkau stated that the findings from the drill cores are unchanged and that no additional drilling has been done.
Freeport mentioned the continued testing of the drill cores in its first-quarter results but provided no further details.
A Canadian mining analyst suggested that Freeport is ensuring thorough testing to determine the presence of gold.
Freeport's announcement on March 26 caused panic selling of shares in Bre-X Minerals Ltd.
Bre-X Minerals Ltd. lost almost C$3 billion in stock market value last month and its shares have been volatile amid rumors.
Bre-X stock traded at C$3.60 on the Toronto Stock Exchange on Thursday, down C2 cents.
Rumors about Freeport Chief Executive Jim Moffett's resignation and preliminary results from an audit were rejected by Bre-X and Freeport officials.

Kellogg Co. will acquire the Lender's Bagels business from Kraft Foods Inc. for $455 million.
Lender's Bagels is based in White Plains, N.Y.
Lender's Bagels is the largest maker of fresh and frozen bagels sold in grocery stores in the United States.
Lender's Bagels has annual sales of about $275 million.
Kraft Foods Inc. is owned by Philip Morris Cos. Inc.
Kellogg Chairman Arnold Langbo stated that Lender's Bagels is a good fit for Kellogg's convenience foods business.
Analysts believe the acquisition will extend Kellogg's reach into the bagel market, which has annual sales estimated at about $2.8 billion.
Kellogg is the world's largest maker of ready-to-eat breakfast cereal.
Kellogg also produces Pop-Tarts, Eggo waffles, and Nutri-Grain bars.
Standard & Poor's Corp. downgraded Kellogg's corporate debt outlook to negative due to concerns about sales and profits.

3Com Corp. proposed a $6.6 billion acquisition of U.S. Robotics Corp.
The acquisition proposal caused a drop in the stocks of 3Com, U.S. Robotics, and other network companies.
3Com's stock fell $4 to $35 and was the most heavily traded issue on Nasdaq.
More than 40 million shares of 3Com changed hands on Nasdaq.
U.S. Robotics' stock dropped $1.875 to $59.125 and was the second-most active share on Nasdaq.
Analysts claimed the proposed stock swap undervalued U.S. Robotics.
Eric Buck, an analyst at Donaldson Lufkin, criticized the terms of the deal.
The offer involved stock and options valued at $7.3 billion.
Peter Swartz, a Salomon analyst, described the deal as a 'take-under' rather than a takeover.
The merger, if approved, would create a company with $5 billion in annual revenues and 12,000 employees.

Foreign airline executives called for Shanghai's new airport to handle both international and domestic flights.
Executives requested early consultations with foreign airlines before the airport's scheduled opening in 1999.
Construction of the new airport in Pudong, which will be the largest in China, begins this month.
The new airport in Pudong will supplement the existing airport at Hongqiao.
Airline representatives indicated uncertainty about which airport they will operate from after 1999.
Many airline representatives believed that Pudong airport would handle international flights and Hongqiao would handle domestic flights.
An unnamed airline executive expressed concerns about limiting either airport to solely international or domestic traffic.
Traffic in Shanghai is congested, but city officials claim it will be eased by a network of elevated highways.
Lu Jianhua, an official with the Pudong airport planning office, stated that both airports would operate international and domestic flights, but final arrangements were not settled.
The first phase of Pudong airport will include a 4,000-metre runway and a main building costing 12 billion yuan, accommodating 20 million passengers and 750,000 tonnes of air cargo.

Opposition leader Milos Zeman asked the Czech parliament to approve a separate resolution regarding a post-World War Two reconciliation pact with Germany.
Deputies in Zeman's Social Democratic party (CSSD) admitted that votes were likely available to pass the deal with Germany without the extra resolution.
The governing coalition has rejected Zeman's demand for an accompanying rider to the reconciliation pact.
Zeman expressed a desire for the parliament to express itself on the declaration as a sovereign state.
Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's conservative coalition is two seats short of a majority in the lower house.
The accord includes German expressions of regret for the Nazi occupation of Czech lands and Czech sorrow for the post-war expulsion of ethnic Germans.
The text of the accord supports Czech membership in the European Union (EU) and the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO).
The accord does not address direct compensation for property seized from expelled Germans.
German politicians have stated that the issue of individual compensation for property remains open despite the inter-governmental declaration.
CSSD vice-chairman Karel Machovec acknowledged that the government likely had enough votes to win the declaration.

Singapore Airlines Ltd (SIA) has taken delivery of a new Boeing 747-400 freighter.
An airline spokesman informed Reuters about the delivery.
The new freighter increases SIA's cargo fleet to five 747-400 freighters and one 747-200 freighter.
A sixth 747-400 freighter is expected to replace the 747-200 in March next year.
SIA's latest 747 freighter arrived at Singapore's Changi airport on November 27.
The new freighter is scheduled to make its first revenue earning flight to San Francisco and Los Angeles.
The date for the first revenue earning flight has not yet been announced.
The new freighter will be used on all SIA's cargo routes worldwide.

Arjo Wiggins Appleton Plc reported a decline in half-year profits.
The company's first half pre-tax profits decreased to 32.3 million pounds from 135.3 million pounds a year ago.
Arjo Wiggins Appleton Plc maintained its interim dividend at 2.9 pence per share.
The company described the first half of 1996 and the second half of 1995 as the worst period since its flotation.
Arjo was demerged from B.A.T Industries in 1990.
Finance director Andrew Shaw stated that prospects for the second half are fragile but may improve.
Arjo's shares fell by 4.5 pence to 181.5 pence.
Pulp prices collapsed from the end of 1995, affecting paper levels.
Margins for carbonless and coated paper in Europe were squeezed.
The company expects to benefit from restructuring efforts in the second half.

The Czech National Bank (CNB) expressed dissatisfaction with the continued firming of the Czech crown.
The CNB stated it has the option to intervene in the market when necessary.
CNB spokesman Martin Svehla indicated that intervention is a normal instrument for the bank.
The Czech crown was fixed at 27.947/dollar and 16.664/mark on Wednesday.
The crown was 5.42 percent over parity with the dollar/mark basket.
The CNB's fixing on Tuesday was at +5.51 percent.
Svehla mentioned that CNB governor Josef Tosovsky stated there is 'no reason' for the crown's current value.
The rise of the crown has been attributed to over 30 billion crowns in recent Eurobond issues.
The trade deficit in the Czech Republic grew to a record 160 billion crowns in 1996.
The CNB has not intervened in the market since February when it widened the fixing corridor.

Sergio Cabrera is a movie director from Colombia.
Cabrera previously participated in guerrilla warfare.
Cabrera believes that Latin American directors can succeed against Hollywood and European film industries.
Cabrera advocates for creating modestly priced films with new perspectives.
Cabrera stated that Latin American directors should approach filmmaking like guerrilla fighters.
Cabrera directed the films 'Estrategia Caracol (Snail Strategy)' and 'Ilona Llega Con La Lluvia (Ilona Arrived In The Rain)'.
Cabrera was a Red Guard during the Cultural Revolution in China at the age of 15.
Cabrera joined the People's Liberation Army (EPL) in Colombia three years after returning from China.
Cabrera fought against government troops in Colombia for four years.
Cabrera's film 'Ilona' received favorable reviews at the Toronto and Sundance film festivals.

Baxter International Inc is comfortable with the First Call consensus 1997 earnings forecast of $2.36 per share.
The 1996 earnings per share for Baxter was $2.11.
Harry Kraemer is the chief financial officer of Baxter International Inc.
Baxter expects 1997 revenues to be in the $6.5-billion range.
Baxter reported revenues of $5.43 billion for 1996.
Baxter anticipates closing its $623-million acquisition of Immuno International AG by mid-year.
Baxter expects to post charges on acquired in-process research and development related to buying Immuno and Research Medical Inc.
The size of the charges related to the acquisitions has not been determined.
Baxter expects to close the $236-million acquisition of Research Medical by the end of the first quarter.
Baxter's gross profit margin was 44.6 percent for the quarter just ended.

LVMH plans to spin off its brewing, food, and burger businesses in a merger between Guinness Plc and Grand Metropolitan Plc.
Analysts are showing sympathy towards LVMH's plan.
Bernard Arnault is the chairman of LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton.
Arnault holds a 14.2 percent stake in Guinness.
Arnault has acquired a 6.29 percent stake in GrandMet through two share raids.
Arnault has spent around 800 million pounds to improve his negotiating position.
Arnault is now the largest shareholder in both Guinness and GrandMet.
The merger aims to create a new group called GMG Brands.
GMG Brands will include brands such as Johnnie Walker, Bell's whisky, Gordon's Gin, Smirnoff Vodka, and Burger King.
Analysts expect GMG Brands to eventually spin off at least Burger King.

AirTouch Communications Inc. agreed to buy U S West Media Group's cellular phone operations for about $4.5 billion in stock and debt.
The acquisition replaces a complex 1994 agreement between AirTouch and U S West.
If the transaction is completed, AirTouch would become the second-largest cellular service provider in the United States.
AirTouch would have 5.3 million customers in 20 states from the West Coast to the Mississippi River.
The companies warned they would cancel the acquisition if Congress passes legislation that closes a corporate tax loophole.
AirTouch would pay about $2.2 billion in stock and assume $2.2 billion of U S West's debt under the agreement.
AirTouch would acquire New Vector and U S West's interest in PrimeCo Personal Communications.
Charles DiSanza, a telecommunications analyst, stated that merging the companies is a good move.
AirTouch shares rose $1 to $24.50 on the New York Stock Exchange.
U S West shares rose 50 cents to $17.75.

Far East traders stated that China is unlikely to need to buy rice on the international market due to flood damage to domestic crops.
No inquiries for rice from China were reported by traders in China, Hong Kong, Singapore, and Thailand.
A Chinese trader in Shanghai ruled out large demand from the central grain reserve, COFCO, or the grain bureaux.
China's Futures Herald newspaper reported that flood damage had reduced the early rice harvest but total output for 1996 was expected to be unaffected.
The increase in the area under rice cultivation in China this year is expected to mitigate the impact of reduced early harvests.
Higher production of other crops is expected to offset the reduction in the early rice harvest.
Rice imports in China require central government approval, and the process for issuing quotas and licenses can take weeks or months.
The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies reported that flooding in Hunan has prevented farmers from planting rice for the autumn harvest.
Thorir Gudmundsson stated that many farmers lost the first crop of rice due to floods and may depend on food aid until the next summer.
Chicago Board of Trade rice futures prices were supported by the notion that China might need to import rice to meet demand.

French oil group Elf Aquitaine signed an oil exploration deal with Azerbaijan.
Azerbaijan is described by France as the next oil Eldorado.
The contract is part of a series of Western oil deals in the Caspian Sea region.
The Caspian Sea contains significant oil reserves despite ethnic conflicts and pipeline disputes.
Elf signed a production sharing contract for the offshore Lenkoran-Talysh Deniz permit with Azeri national oil firm Socar.
The contract was signed in the presence of Azeri President Haydar Aliyev and French President Jacques Chirac.
Aliyev stated the pact is worth $1.5 billion and raises total planned investments in Azeri petroleum to $15 billion.
The field is expected to produce 350 million barrels of oil.
Elf will hold a 65 percent stake as operator in the field, while Socar will have 25 percent.
Elf's smaller rival Total SA has a 10 percent stake in the project.

Paccar Inc. is the maker of Kenworth, Peterbilt, and Foden heavy-duty trucks.
Paccar reported fourth-quarter profits of $62.5 million, or $1.61 per share, for the quarter ended December 31.
Paccar's fourth-quarter profits decreased from $65.1 million, or $1.67 per share, a year earlier.
Paccar's sales increased to $1.2 billion from $1.1 billion.
Paccar's earnings exceeded Wall Street expectations of $1.23 per share.
Paccar's stock rose by $2.25 to $69.75 in afternoon Nasdaq trading.
Analyst Paul Latta credited Paccar's better-than-expected results to its acquisition of DAF Trucks N.V.
Paccar completed the acquisition of DAF Trucks N.V. in November for $543.8 million.
Paccar's net income for the year fell to $201 million, or $5.17 per share, from $252.8 million, or $6.50 per share, in 1995.
Paccar's sales for the year dropped to $4.3 billion from $4.6 billion.

Leading cruise ship operators aim to replicate their U.S. successes in international markets.
Top industry executives believe Europe and Asia are promising markets for Carnival Corp and Royal Caribbean Cruises Ltd.
The North American leisure cruise business has significantly grown over the past three decades.
Tim Harris, chairman of P&O/Princess Cruises, stated that North American lines can grow internationally if they recognize cultural and business differences.
North American cruise lines are currently experiencing strong domestic business, particularly in the Caribbean and Alaska.
Carnival Cruise Lines reported a 37 percent increase in bookings over three months, attributed to a 13 percent rise in shipboard berths.
Most customers of North American cruise lines are from the U.S. and Canada, and the offerings are primarily American.
Executives suggest that cruise offerings will need to be tailored to local tastes in Asia and Europe.
Richard Sasso, president of Celebrity Cruises Inc, emphasized the importance of matching ships, locations, and food to local preferences.
Carnival and Royal Caribbean are already active in international markets, employing different strategies for their operations.

U.S. and Chinese officials have started textile trade talks.
The talks are the last chance to reach a deal before a Friday deadline.
Top U.S. textile negotiator Rita Hayes stated that the talks were productive.
Hayes met Chinese trade officials for the first of three scheduled days of talks.
The talks aim to extend a bilateral textile accord and resolve a dispute over U.S. penalties on Chinese textile imports.
The 1994 Sino-U.S. textile accord was set to expire on December 31 last year but was extended by one month.
Hayes indicated that there are still many issues to resolve before reaching an agreement.
The deadline for reaching an agreement is January 31, with no further extensions.
Washington imposed $19 million in penalties on Chinese textile imports last September.
China has threatened to retaliate by banning imports of some U.S. textiles but has delayed action for further talks.

Quaker Oats Co may take a write-down of up to $1.0 billion for its Snapple beverage business.
Analysts stated that the write-down charge may not appear in Quaker's fourth quarter earnings report.
BT Securities analyst John O'Neil estimated the write-down could be close to $1.0 billion.
Credit Suisse First Boston analyst Michael Mauboussin indicated a reasonably high probability of a write-down.
Quaker spokesman Ronald Bottrell confirmed that a review of Snapple operations is ongoing.
Bottrell declined to comment on whether Quaker plans to take a charge for Snapple.
In November, Quaker announced it would review Snapple to determine if a charge was necessary.
Sanford Bernstein analyst Steven Galbraith stated that Quaker is compelled to take a charge for Snapple.
Galbraith suggested that Quaker could avoid a write-down if it sold Snapple along with Gatorade.
Speculation exists that Quaker is considering selling both Snapple and Gatorade.

Gerard Mestrallet is the head of Cie de Suez.
Mestrallet is considering a merger with Lyonnaise des Eaux.
The market anticipates that Mestrallet will lead the new merged group.
Brokers believe that Suez and Lyonnaise will merge to create a utilities group with an estimated market capitalisation of 79 billion francs ($13.9 billion).
Suez has a significant cash reserve and 50 billion francs in capital but lacks industrial identity.
Jerome Monod, chairman of Lyonnaise, is preparing for retirement.
A merger would financially strengthen Lyonnaise and provide new leadership.
Mestrallet is favored to lead the merged group after taking over Suez two years ago.
Mestrallet previously worked at Suez's Belgian unit, Societe Generale de Belgique (SGB).
Guy de Panafieu is the number two to Monod at Lyonnaise and is also a graduate of ENA.

Regulators will host an auction on Tuesday for radio service licenses.
Supporters claim the auction will introduce a new nationwide radio service.
Critics argue the auction may cost U.S. taxpayers millions in lost revenue.
Two licenses for coast-to-coast satellite radio programming are available.
Digital radio will provide CD-quality sound and specialized programming.
William Caldwell is the president of Digital Satellite Broadcasting Corp.
The FCC limited the auction to four companies that applied by the end of 1992.
Chairman Reed Hundt and Commissioner Susan Ness favored opening the auction to all bidders.
Commissioner Rachelle Chong argued that limiting the auction was fair to the four applicants.
Digital radio is expected to be subscription-based, costing about $10 a month.

Thailand's banking sector experienced an implosion.
There are concerns about banks' property exposure in Hong Kong.
Capital inflows into Hong Kong have increased due to optimism about its reversion to China.
Bank loans for property in Hong Kong have significantly increased.
Soaring property prices are viewed as a confidence indicator for Hong Kong.
Hugh Peyman from Dresdner Kleinwort Benson expressed concerns about the assumptions of Hong Kong bankers regarding money supply.
David Lui from Schroder Securities warned that rising property prices could affect the financial sector's soundness.
The Hong Kong Monetary Authority indicated that additional mortgage lending restraints might be necessary.
Outstanding property lending in Hong Kong has increased by 26 percent in one year.
Property and construction account for 47 percent of all lending in Hong Kong.

China indicated ethnic unrest in Xinjiang on Thursday.
Vice-Premier Li Lanqing called for unity in Xinjiang.
Li's remarks were reported by the People's Daily.
Li did not directly reference the bombings in Urumqi on February 25.
The bombings occurred on the day of funeral rites for Deng Xiaoping.
At least 20 ethnic Uighurs were arrested in Urumqi and Yining.
Exiled Uighur nationalists reported the arrests from Almaty.
Three bombs exploded on public buses in Urumqi on February 25.
The Xinjiang Daily reported arrests of individuals suspected of planting bombs.
Wang Hanbin introduced revisions to China's criminal law regarding ethnic hatred.

Hong Kong's government and business community welcomed U.S. President Bill Clinton's decision to renew China's trade privileges.
Hong Kong's government and business community hope the U.S. Congress will not oppose the renewal of China's trade privileges.
The extension of China's Most Favoured Nation (MFN) trading status is important to Hong Kong as it prepares for its return to Chinese rule on July 1.
Erica Ng is the assistant manager of international affairs at the Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce.
Erica Ng stated that the chamber is very happy about the renewal of China's MFN status.
Christopher Hammerbeck is the executive director of the British Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong.
Christopher Hammerbeck expressed that the decision still requires endorsement by Congress.
Denise Yue is the Secretary for Trade and Industry in Hong Kong.
Denise Yue stated that the Hong Kong government will continue to lobby Congress regarding China's trade privileges.
Frank Martin is the president of the American Chamber of Commerce (AmCham) in Hong Kong.

Bass sold 47 Holiday Inn hotels in North America to Bristol Hotel Co.
The sale is part of Bass's plan to build a global franchise business.
Bass finance director Richard North stated that franchising is their primary business.
Owning and managing hotels is a means of supporting Bass's franchising operation.
Bass believes it is no longer necessary to own and manage hotels in the U.S.
The sale of the hotels and management contracts was worth $659 million.
Bristol will spend $150 million on refurbishing the properties over the next three years.
The 61 hotels transferred generated profits of $69 million in the year to September 30.
Holiday Inn franchisees in the U.S. receive about 33 percent of their occupancy through the Holiday Inn reservation system.
Bass owns 60 Holiday Inn hotels in Europe, the Middle East, and Africa, and 39 in the Asia-Pacific region.

Deng Xiaoping died at the age of 92 on Wednesday.
Deng Xiaoping was the architect of China's economic reforms.
Jiang Zemin is Deng Xiaoping's hand-picked successor and the current President and Communist Party chief of China.
China's economy is described as being in its best shape in years.
China has experienced strong economic growth and has inflation in check.
China's foreign exchange reserves amount to $105 billion.
Lin Qingsong is an economist at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences.
Lin Qingsong expressed optimism about China's economic situation.
China's economic growth rate was 9.7 percent last year.
Approximately 75 percent of China's state firms lost money last year.

The U.S. government is updating thousands of computer systems and software programs to address the year 2000 problem.
Sally Katzen is coordinating the repair effort as the administrator of the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs in the Office of Management and Budget.
Sally Katzen expressed confidence that all major systems will be fixed.
Legislators in Congress are interested in the year 2000 problem and are encouraging agencies to take action.
Some government agencies are aware of the year 2000 problem, while others, such as the air traffic control system, are raising concerns.
Representative Steve Horn stated that Congress will continue to address the year 2000 problem until it is resolved.
Steve Horn is the chairman of the Government Reform Committee's Management, Information and Technology sub-committee.
The sub-committee has received testimony from government and private-sector experts regarding the year 2000 problem.
A recent survey indicated that all government agencies are aware of the year 2000 problem and most are prepared to implement fixes.
The Defence Department and the Social Security Administration have extensive plans to address the year 2000 problem before December 31, 1999.

TrizecHahn Corp is based in Canada.
Dieter Bock is a German businessman.
TrizecHahn Corp and Dieter Bock announced a European property alliance.
Analysts believe the alliance indicates increasing confidence in the UK and European property market.
TrizecHahn has $6.0 billion in assets and $1.2 billion in uncommitted capital.
TrizecHahn plans to buy property projects from Bock's Advanta Management AG for approximately $147 million.
The acquisitions will be financed by issuing subordinate voting shares to Bock, assuming development liabilities, and through construction financing.
Dieter Bock will become president of TrizecHahn Europe and a director of the company with an equity stake of around four percent.
Bock will resign as non-executive deputy chairman of Lonrho Plc and as a director of the British-based trading and hotels conglomerate.
The partnership aims to expand TrizecHahn's operations outside North America.

James Hardie Industries Ltd posted weaker annual profits on Wednesday.
James Hardie forecast that its expanding U.S. fibre cement and gypsum units would drive a profit surge in 1997/98.
Keith Barton is the managing director of James Hardie.
Barton stated that James Hardie has the production capacity to meet U.S. market demand for the first time in several years.
Barton expects strong growth in U.S. sales and earnings to continue in the year ahead if current trading conditions prevail.
James Hardie's net profit increased to A$83 million in the year to March 31 from A$32.2 million in 1995/96.
The increase in net profit was largely due to a A$31.7 million abnormal profit from asset sales.
Profit before abnormals fell 12.3 percent to A$51.3 million due to lower Australasian building materials profits.
James Hardie's Australian operations reported a pre-tax loss of A$800,000 in 1996/97, down from a profit of A$33.8 million in 1995/96.
New Zealand profits fell eight percent to A$31.9 million.

Toronto is Canada's largest city.
A citizens revolt has emerged against Ontario's ruling Conservatives.
Ontario's Conservative Premier is Mike Harris.
Harris proposes merging Toronto and six neighboring municipalities into a single 'megacity'.
The proposed 'megacity' would have a population of 2.4 million people.
The new city would represent about 8 percent of Canada's total population of 30 million.
Harris plans to change how public services are delivered and funded.
Opponents of the plan fear it will increase taxes and lead to urban decay.
Toronto mayor Barbara Hall stated that government is elected by the people for the people.
The recent referendum showed that residents voted three to one against the merger.

Britain's double-decker bus is involved in environmental experiments.
A London bus operator has collaborated with inventor Hassan Assali for two years.
Hassan Assali claims to have a solution for diesel-based pollution fumes.
Assali's invention is an oil recycler that reportedly cuts pollution levels by 50 percent.
The oil recycler saves lubricating oil by recycling it six to ten times.
Assali is the managing director of Pinmore, the company behind the recycler.
The Pinmore recycler prototype was developed over six years with significant investment.
The recycler is manufactured in Huzhan province, China, and has sold 6,000 units.
Customers include an Algerian bus company and Saudi Arabia's frontier guards.
MTL publicly endorsed the recycler after successful tests on its buses.

Computer Associates International Inc shares fell six percent on Wednesday.
Analysts attributed the decline to concerns over a secular decline in mainframe revenues.
The company had previously warned that revenues were unlikely to meet expectations due to sales issues in Europe.
By midday Wednesday, the stock price had decreased by three points to 43.
The stock was the second most active issue on the NYSE.
Analysts noted that CA's decline may be related to broader weakness in the mainframe market.
International Business Machines Corp reported disappointing growth in its hardware business during the December quarter.
IBM is the world's dominant supplier of mainframe software.
Computer Associates is a leading independent supplier of software for mainframe machines.
Analyst Chris Mortenson reported that mainframe revenues had fallen eight percent in the December quarter.

China's stock markets began returning to normal on Friday.
All indices closed up in steady trade after the negative impact of Deng Xiaoping's death faded.
Retail investors and institutions began building positions reflecting sentiment that Deng's death would benefit the markets in the longer term.
At the close on Friday, Shanghai's foreign currency B share index rose 0.894 points, or 1.38 percent, to 65.569 points.
The domestic A share index closed at a year high of 1,063.276, rising 55.545 points, or 5.51 percent.
In Shenzhen, the B share index rose 7.43 points, or 5.18 percent, to 150.96.
The A share index in Shenzhen rose 8.68 points, or 2.48 percent, to 359.28.
Shanghai brokers convened meetings on Thursday to discuss maintaining normal market operations.
Some analysts suspected the markets were receiving support from institutions to prevent major movements after Deng's death.
The relatively short mourning period before Deng's funeral indicated China's desire to dispel gloom quickly.

The Czech Republic's plan to diversify natural gas supplies has been delayed for several weeks.
The Industry and Trade Ministry announced the delay on Tuesday.
Miroslav Konvalina is the spokesman for the Industry and Trade Ministry.
The plan was expected to be submitted to the government in January.
No reason for the delay was provided by Konvalina.
The government is considering limited deliveries from Norway.
The Ministry is developing four options for securing gas supplies.
Russia is expected to remain the dominant supplier regardless of the chosen plan.
One option involves purchasing all natural gas from Gazprom with a long-term agreement until 2016.
The Czech Republic consumes around eight to nine billion cubic metres of natural gas per year.

Hong Kong Air Cargo Terminals Limited (HACTL) set four new handling records during December.
HACTL's managing director is Anthony Charter.
Imports were strong during the pre-Christmas peak season.
A new daily import handling record of 2,661 tonnes was set on December 26.
A new weekly import record of 15,720 tonnes was recorded between December 16 and 22.
December 2023 was a record month for imports with 67,572 tonnes landing at Kai Tak airport.
On December 15, a new daily record for combined imports and exports of 5,788 tonnes was set.
HACTL's long-range forecast is for 8 percent growth this year.
Anthony Charter personally thinks growth may reach 10 percent.
HACTL has a monopoly on all air cargo handling at Kai Tak airport.

National Westminster Bank Plc will perform further share repurchases if it generates more surplus capital.
Derek Wanless is the chief executive of National Westminster Bank Plc.
Some analysts expected NatWest to buy back 28 million shares costing approximately 220 million stg.
NatWest did not announce a share buyback when it posted its 1996 results.
Derek Wanless stated that if surplus capital is available, it will be returned to shareholders.
NatWest will ask shareholders to return its buy-back mandate to 100 million shares at its AGM in April.
NatWest's tier one capital ratio was 6.7 percent at the end of 1996.
NatWest generated and used a large amount of capital on improving systems and technology and on acquisitions in 1996.
NatWest UK saw a six percent rise in income and a two percent fall in costs in 1996.
NatWest posted a pre-tax profit of 1.12 billion stg in 1996, down from 1.75 billion in 1995.

President Emil Constantinescu stated that military modernisation costs were Romania's only obstacle to full NATO membership.
Constantinescu expressed that Romania should still be named in the first wave of new NATO members.
During a visit to Radio Free Europe headquarters in Prague, Constantinescu mentioned that Romania had met all NATO membership criteria except for military equipment upgrades.
Constantinescu indicated that Romania's nomination in the first wave would be followed by effective integration once all conditions were fulfilled.
Romania needs to fulfill the capacity to support the costs of modernising its military equipment.
Romania, with support from France, Spain, and Italy, has intensified diplomatic efforts to be among the first ex-communist states invited to join NATO.
Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic are expected to be named as new NATO members.
Constantinescu claimed that Romania saw no alternative to NATO integration and should be part of the first group.
Romania is attempting to link its NATO bid with Hungary's, having signed an agreement to form a joint military battalion.
Constantinescu stated that Romania now meets NATO's membership criteria on democracy and human rights.

Former Colombian president Virgilio Barco Vargas died at the age of 75 in a Bogota clinic.
Barco battled stomach cancer and Alzheimer's disease for a year before his death.
Barco served as president of Colombia from 1986 to 1990.
President Ernesto Samper expressed a sense of loss for Barco in a radio broadcast tribute.
Samper described Barco as a man of firm convictions and dedicated to certain principles.
Barco's body was scheduled to lie in state at the national Congress building.
The government of Norte de Santander declared three days of mourning for Barco.
Barco was born in 1921 in Cucuta, Colombia, near the border with Venezuela.
He graduated from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology with a degree in civil engineering and a doctorate in economic science.
Barco was married to an American and was fluent in English.

Polaris Industries Inc. is known for its snowmobiles.
Polaris will begin building motorcycles.
No major U.S. company other than Harley-Davidson Inc. has entered the motorcycle market in 40 years.
Polaris is developing a highway cruiser motorcycle named Victory, which will be available in spring 1998.
The engine for the Victory motorcycle was designed in the USA and will be made in the USA.
Matt Parks will be the general manager of the new Polaris motorcycles unit.
Polaris is the world's largest maker of snowmobiles and among the top three makers of all-terrain vehicles and personal watercraft.
Polaris has competed successfully against Honda, Yamaha, Kawasaki, and Suzuki in its other businesses.
The cruiser motorcycle will compete with Harley's machines and similar heavy bikes from Honda and others.
Polaris expects its existing customers, many of whom are already active motorcyclists, to be among the early buyers.

Carlton Communications Plc reported an 11 percent rise in half-year earnings.
The rise in earnings was attributed to strong growth in advertising revenue.
Carlton operates ITV commercial television licences for London, the English Midlands, and the west of England.
Pre-tax profits increased to 158.6 million pounds from 143.3 million pounds after a one-off loss of around 4.0 million pounds.
The half-year dividend was raised by 12 percent to 4.9 pence.
Chairman Michael Green stated that the group would continue to invest in businesses and boost prospects.
Carlton's shares had been underperforming the market by around 15 percent in the last three months.
By mid-morning, Carlton's stock price increased by 18.5 pence to 517.5 pence.
Carlton's core broadcast business saw a 19 percent rise in operating profits to 72.6 million pounds.
Carlton's share of ITV's advertising revenue increased to 32.58 percent from 31.75 percent.

Toronto stocks closed weaker on Thursday after a sell-off led by New York.
The Toronto Stock Exchange's 300 Composite Index lost 43.79 points to settle at 6205.07.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average plunged 92.75 points to reach 6927.38.
The Toronto Stock Exchange had its heaviest trading session with 169.4 million shares traded worth C$2.97 billion.
The 300 index did not cross the key support mark of 6175 points.
Ron Meisels stated that the index is still above the break-out level.
The gold group in Toronto rose 3.23 percent due to surging bullion prices on COMEX.
April gold closed $5.00 higher at $352.70 per ounce.
All of Toronto's 14 sub-indices lost ground except for golds and retail.
Declining stocks outnumbered advancing ones 518 to 515, with 268 stocks trading flat.

China has up to a million tonnes of corn rotting in silos in the country's north.
Traders reported that this year is expected to be a major disaster for corn exports.
An estimated 500,000 to one million tonnes of corn is stored in northern silos in anticipation of exports.
Corn is predominantly grown in China's far northeastern provinces of Heilongjiang, Jilin, and Liaoning.
Corn began moving to northern ports, particularly Dalian, around May.
Traders anticipated that two million tonnes of corn would be permissioned for export.
Concerns about national food security and domestic prices have kept China out of the world corn market.
Corn and rice exports were banned in December 1994 due to low stock levels.
China imported a total of 5.18 million tonnes of corn in 1995.
Corn imports in the first five months of 1996 were 400,000 tonnes.

French state agencies met to approve an 11 billion franc capital injection for Thomson SA.
The French government is reviewing options for reviving the sale of Thomson SA.
Thomson labour unions and other labour groups are planning a demonstration in Paris.
The demonstration is to demand the total cancellation of Thomson's privatisation.
The privatisation of Thomson was suspended earlier this week.
Finance Minister Jean Arthuis is under political pressure to restore France's reputation in international markets.
Arthuis is working on how to relaunch the sale process for Thomson SA.
The decision to suspend the privatisation outraged South Korea.
The independent Privatisation Commission did not agree with the terms of the planned sale of Thomson Multimedia to Daewoo Electronics.
State shareholders at Thomson's Paris headquarters held an extraordinary meeting to vote on the capital increase.

Advanced Technology Laboratories Inc's chairman and chief executive expects 1997 revenues to rise six to seven percent from $329.7 million generated in 1996.
Dennis Fill stated in an interview that he is comfortable with analyst estimates that the company would earn $1.75 to $1.90 a share in 1997.
In 1996, Advanced Technology Laboratories Inc earned $1.46 per share, excluding non-recurring items.
The gross profit margin is expected to rise to about 51 percent of revenues in 1997 from 48.9 percent in 1996.
Dennis Fill mentioned that the increase in gross profit margin provides customers with great flexibility and lower costs.
Fill stated that the improvement in gross profit margin brings a great enhancement in capability to the midrange market.
The new HDI 1000 includes a WebLink component that allows users to send images directly over the Internet.
The HDI 1000 does not require passing images through a computer workstation.
The HDI 1000 is intended for general ultrasound applications, excluding cardiovascular uses.
The HDI 1000 is expected to sell for $50,000 to $100,000 depending on features, compared to $135,000 to $250,000 for the HDI 3000.

Tobacco-industry lawyers are involved in the $5 billion Broin secondhand smoke case.
Dade County Circuit Court Judge Robert Kaye criticized the tobacco lawyers for confusing prospective jurors with trick questions.
Judge Kaye stated that it is impossible to find a fully neutral jury due to the controversial nature of smoking.
Florida law requires jurors to set aside their prejudices and decide based on the evidence presented.
Stanley Rosenblatt is an attorney representing 60,000 sick flight attendants in the Broin class-action suit.
Rosenblatt described the tactics used by tobacco lawyers as mind games aimed at finding uninformed jurors.
A young musician testified that her voice was harmed by secondhand smoke while singing in nightclubs.
The musician stated she could set aside her belief that cigarettes should be banned and decide based on the evidence.
Judge Kaye denied a request from tobacco lawyers to dismiss the musician as prejudiced against cigarette makers.
Six prospective jurors survived the initial questioning, with eleven total having passed the initial round.

Ameritech Corp has a three-part strategy to maintain earnings growth despite new competitors entering its midwest region.
Ameritech has strengthened its core local calling business.
Ameritech has entered new businesses such as cable TV and security to add value to its network.
Ameritech has sought profitable niches abroad.
Chief Executive Richard Notebaert stated that the strategies started three years ago are effective.
Notebaert acknowledged that costs from new competitors would be significant but would not hinder growth below double-digit earnings.
Ameritech has not pursued mergers as it has not found any business combinations that would add value for shareholders.
Ameritech focuses on software calling features like call-waiting and caller ID instead of promoting extra lines.
Ameritech's growth in lines has decreased from 4.5 percent to 3.5 percent per year.
Ameritech has entered the security business, acquiring SecurityLink in 1994 and National Guardian in 1995, and has 367,000 users.

Interstate Bakeries Corp chairman Charles Sullivan supports analysts' earnings estimates of $0.35-$0.40 a share for the company's third quarter.
The timeframe for the earnings estimates has been corrected from fiscal 1997.
Sullivan stated that the company is not uncomfortable with the analysts' estimates.
In the third quarter of the previous year, the company earned $0.11 a share.
Sullivan indicated that anticipated growth in third quarter earnings is due to reduced costs, higher revenues, and increased sales of branded products.
Interstate Bakeries Corp is the largest baker and distributor of fresh bakery products in the United States.
The company has brands including Wonder, Hostess, and Dolly Madison.
Interstate plans to extend its brand lines with new products aimed at children and adults.
The company has begun rolling out a fat-free Wonder bread, which is expected to appeal to older consumers.
Interstate is seeking acquisitions in a consolidating industry and plans to acquire an existing bakery operation west of the Mississippi River.

Airbus Industrie criticized Delta Air Lines Inc.'s exclusive deal with Boeing Co. as anti-competitive.
Delta Air Lines Inc. announced it would buy new aircraft exclusively from Boeing Co. for the next 25 years.
Delta Air Lines Inc. placed a $6.7 billion order for 106 Boeing aircraft.
The total number of aircraft Delta could acquire, including options, is 644.
The Delta deal could be worth more than $15 billion.
American Airlines previously entered into a similar exclusive deal with Boeing.
An Airbus spokeswoman stated that Boeing's exclusive deals could harm competition.
The Airbus spokeswoman claimed that if Airbus is forced out of the market, prices would increase.
Boeing holds approximately 60 percent of the global civil aircraft market.
Airbus is a consortium of four European companies and is in talks to convert into a limited liability company by 1999.

Companies that won wireless phone licenses at last year's $10.2 billion federal auction are facing financial strains.
NextWave Telecom Inc. and Pocket Communications Inc. are among the top bidders requesting a more lenient payment timetable from the government.
NextWave's winning bids totaled $4.7 billion, while Pocket's bids amounted to $1.4 billion.
The bids have become loans from the government, with the winners paying interest on the money owed for the licenses.
The companies want to make interest payments annually instead of quarterly.
The additional time for payments would help the companies raise funds to build personal communications services (PCS) systems.
The winners of the 1996 Federal Communication Commission auction paid more than double the price paid by big carriers like AT&T Corp. in 1995.
Industry officials want the FCC to clarify certain repayment rules and for the Treasury Department to take over payment collection.
Attorney Lynn Charytan stated that making it easier for companies to pay would make them more attractive to investors.
NextWave, Pocket, and seven other PCS winners requested the FCC to allow annual interest payments to provide more flexibility in accessing financial markets.

China has tightened controls on red chip shares.
Economists believe China is ready to confront its structural economic problems.
Geoff Lewis is the chief economist with Dresdner Kleinwort Benson.
Lewis wrote that economic and political circumstances are ripe for new policy initiatives after Deng Xiaoping's death.
Lewis did not expect major policy announcements before Hong Kong's July 1 return to Chinese rule.
China announced new measures to tighten controls on red chips after a significant gain in the Hang Seng index.
The Hang Seng index gained 647.87 points, or 4.5 percent, reaching a record of 15,154.36.
China will require Chinese-controlled companies to obtain approvals before listing overseas.
Companies will need approvals for transfers of domestic assets into listed affiliates.
Michael Taylor, an economist with W.I. Carr, stated that disinflationary pressures are affecting China and the region.

Norwich Union is a British insurer.
Norwich Union will start trading its shares on the stock market on Monday.
The company has more than seven million customers.
Norwich Union is likely to be valued at around six billion pounds upon flotation.
Norwich Union will be Britain's third-largest quoted insurer.
Nearly three million Norwich policyholders will share 1.3 billion free shares under the flotation plans.
Norwich Union aims to raise 1.75 billion pounds through a public and members' offer of new shares.
Members have the opportunity to buy further shares at a 25 pence discount.
Norwich Union expects the public offer to be priced between 240 pence and 290 pence per share.
Norwich Union announced it was clawing back 400 million pounds worth of shares from the public offering to satisfy demand.

Tung Chee-hwa is the future leader of Hong Kong.
Tung Chee-hwa assured Philippine Foreign Secretary Domingo Siazon that Filipino workers will be allowed to stay in Hong Kong after its reversion to Chinese rule on July 1.
Domingo Siazon arrived in Hong Kong late on Thursday.
Siazon informed Tung of the Philippines' decision to waive visa requirements for Hong Kong passport holders visiting the Philippines.
Hong Kong will become a Special Administrative Region under Chinese rule at midnight on June 30.
Nearly 140,000 Philippine workers, mainly maids, live in Hong Kong.
Many Filipinos fear expulsion and replacement by domestic servants from mainland China after Hong Kong becomes part of China.
Siazon stated that concerns about the status of Filipino workers in Hong Kong are unwarranted.
An estimated seven million Filipinos working abroad remit about US$7 billion each year back to the Philippines.
Siazon met with Governor Chris Patten and Financial Secretary Donald Tsang during his visit.

LASMO Plc reported profits nearly doubled in 1996.
LASMO reported after-tax profits of 67 million pounds, up from 34 million pounds.
LASMO declared a dividend of 2.0p, up from 1.25p.
The profit figures were in line with broker forecasts of 64 to 75 million pounds.
LASMO shares were up 4-1/2p at 243-1/2p before the last hour of trading in London.
Chief executive Joe Darby stated that oil prices are expected to weaken in the short term but will not fall below $15 or $16 a barrel.
LASMO is planning on an average oil price of $19 for the year on Brent.
Average oil prices rose to $18.72 in 1996 from $17.09 in 1995.
LASMO reported operating costs of 2.87 pounds on average per barrel produced in 1996, down from 3.17 pounds in 1995.
LASMO's peak production in 1996 was supported by production from Indonesia and new British oil fields.

China celebrated the 100-day mark for the recovery of Hong Kong on a Sunday.
China praised late leader Deng Xiaoping for his role in ending over a century of colonial rule.
Hundreds of people gathered near Tiananmen Square in Beijing to watch a countdown clock.
The countdown clock indicated 100 days until Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule on July 1.
Official newspapers reported on the end of British colonial rule as per a Sino-British accord signed in 1984.
The Guangming Daily stated that the hopes of generations would be realized in 100 days.
The People's Daily highlighted Deng Xiaoping's contributions to the transfer of power in Hong Kong.
Deng Xiaoping guided China's negotiations with Britain and proposed the 'one country, two systems' formula.
A crowd in Beijing celebrated the countdown, with students waving banners and chanting slogans.
China ceded Hong Kong island to Britain in 1842 under the Treaty of Nanjing after the Opium War.

The Prague Stock Exchange's 1997 bull run halted on Thursday as investors took profits.
Analysts predicted that prices would continue falling in the short-term.
The PX50 index closed at 613.6 on Thursday, down 14.0 points or 2.23 percent.
The PX50 index had reached a two-year high of 629.0 on Tuesday.
SPT Telecom a.s., CEZ a.s., and Komercni Banka a.s. were the three biggest issues leading the market lower.
Each of the three biggest issues fell more than 2.2 percent at the fix.
Jan Sykora of brokers Wood and Company stated that the market is thin and profit-taking causes it to collapse.
Analysts expect Komercni Banka a.s. to be hardest hit among blue chips after rising over 25 percent since the start of the year.
Komercni Banka a.s. closed down 4.9 percent on Thursday.
Czech authorities are taking steps to increase transparency and boost investor confidence in the capital markets.

Britain's opposition Labour party stated that problems at Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM) could have been uncovered earlier.
Alistair Darling, shadow chief secretary to the Treasury, expressed that the problem was not determined as soon as it should have been.
Darling warned that alarm bells ought to be ringing in all major financial institutions.
Trading in three funds worth an estimated 1.4 billion pounds was suspended when MGAM disclosed suspected irregularities.
The problems at MGAM are related to the valuation of speculative unlisted high-technology stocks held in the funds.
Trading in the three funds resumed after a 180 million pound cash injection by Deutsche Bank.
Peter Young, the fund manager of two of the funds, was suspended and an injunction was obtained to freeze his assets.
An in-depth probe by the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation (IMRO) is underway to determine compensation for 90,000 investors.
Darling indicated that the problems at MGAM highlighted imperfections in the regulatory system.
The Labour party will not make recommendations on the latest episode until IMRO completes its investigation.

Australian Treasurer Peter Costello announced that he would not allow a big bank merger until parts of the banking sector became more competitive.
Costello's announcement affected the takeover premium built into Westpac Banking Corp's share price.
National Australia Bank's share price increased by 2.5 percent following Costello's announcement.
Investors were pleased that National Australia Bank would not have to issue shares to finance a takeover.
A senior Sydney bank analyst stated that the market viewed National Australia Bank's situation positively due to the avoidance of share dilution.
Macquarie Equities analyst Graham Maloney noted that National Australia Bank was previously underpriced.
National Australia Bank closed at A$16.11 after Costello's announcement.
Westpac Banking Corp closed down at A$6.67, while ANZ Banking Group Ltd closed down at A$7.89.
Analysts indicated that Costello's comments about ending the ban on foreign takeovers could mitigate some disappointment in the sector.
J.B. Were, head of research at Craig Drummond, mentioned that Westpac and ANZ were not expensive by global standards.

Freeport-McMoRan Copper & Gold Inc. withdrew from the Busang gold project.
The withdrawal occurred after an independent report on Busang was released by Bre-X Minerals Ltd.
Freeport's own test results from the Busang site were poor.
The report by Strathcona Mineral Services Ltd. confirmed Freeport's findings.
The Busang discovery was claimed by Bre-X to be the richest find of the century.
The Strathcona report stated that the falsification of data was unprecedented in mining history.
Strathcona found evidence of tampering with Bre-X's core samples.
Strathcona's tests revealed only trace amounts of gold at the Busang site.
Freeport's Chief Executive Jim Bob Moffett expressed disappointment over the findings.
Nusamba Group, linked to Indonesian President Suharto, also withdrew from the Busang project.

British defence to electronics giant General Electric Company signalled a shift away from the management legacy of ex-chief Lord Weinstock.
Zafar Khan, an analyst at SocGen, stated that GEC has created a flatter structure with divisional heads reporting directly to George Simpson.
George Simpson succeeded Lord Weinstock as managing director of GEC in September.
GEC announced it would halve the number of its corporate divisions to five key business units: GEC Alsthom, GEC Marconi, GPT, GEC USA, and the industrial group of businesses.
The newly separated industrial group includes the industrial apparatus unit.
GEC created a central committee with representatives from finance, legal affairs, strategic planning, personnel affairs, marketing, and technical issues.
Analysts believe the move updated GEC's corporate structure and created a clearer chain of command.
GEC grouped together its main U.S. businesses, including Picker International, Gilbarco, and Videojet.
An analyst reported that the regrouping did not necessarily indicate that industrials were being separated for sale.
GEC finance director David Newlands stated that the group had received multiple offers mostly above book value.

The president and 15 board members at Nomura Securities Co Ltd will resign due to a racketeering scandal.
Masashi Suzuki is the president of Nomura Securities Co Ltd and was appointed one month ago.
The resignation of Suzuki's predecessor occurred when the racketeering affair came to light.
Prosecutors and the securities watchdog are investigating whether Nomura paid off a racketeer known as 'sokaiya'.
Junichi Ujiie is a managing director at Nomura and will become president on May 1.
Ujiie aims to establish a more open management system based on clear rules.
An analyst, Yushiro Ikuyo, believes the resignation of executives will positively impact Nomura's corporate culture.
Nomura was previously punished by regulators in 1991 for improperly favoring certain clients.
Hideo Sakamaki resigned as president of Nomura last month when the scandal broke.
Sakamaki testified that Nomura paid more than 70 million yen via stock deals into accounts linked to a racketeer.

China Minsheng Banking Corp is China's first and only non-state bank.
The bank plans major growth in 1997.
China Minsheng Banking Corp will remain a niche player compared to state banks.
The bank was founded in Beijing a year ago.
The bank opened branches in Shanghai and Guangzhou last month.
The bank plans to open branches in at least six other Chinese cities within the next 12 months.
The planned cities for new branches include Shenzhen, Dalian, Hangzhou, Wuhan, Chengdu, and either Qingdao or Jinan.
The bank's growth plans do not pose a threat to state banks.
The Minsheng Bank has 59 shareholders, mostly private Chinese firms.
The bank had a profit of 11 million yuan in its first year and has over seven billion yuan in assets.

A debate in the Czech parliament over a post-World War Two reconciliation agreement with Germany continued into a third day.
Small opposition parties are attempting to obstruct a vote on the Czech-German declaration.
The Czech-German declaration aims to resolve political questions related to World War Two and its aftermath.
Supporters of the declaration are trying to limit the debate.
The ultra-right Czech Republican Party opposes the declaration and has submitted a counter-declaration.
Republican deputy Josef Krejsa proposed 305 billion marks in compensation for the Nazi occupation of Czech lands.
Krejsa's proposal includes freezing all German assets in the Czech Republic until compensation is paid.
Political analysts believe the Republican initiative has little chance of approval.
The Czech-German declaration expresses regret for the Nazi occupation and sorrow for the expulsion of ethnic Germans.
The declaration establishes a fund for compensating victims of Nazi aggression but does not address direct compensation for expropriated ethnic German property.

Martinair has begun a freighter service between Guangzhou and Amsterdam.
Walter Tseng is the Far East general manager of Martinair.
Tseng expects the new service to be gradually built up after initial flights on December 20 and 29.
The first two flights included local cargo from Guangzhou, cargo from Hong Kong, and additional cargo from Bangkok.
Guangzhou is considered less significant than Hong Kong as an entry point for cargo.
Tseng noted that competition from Hong Kong makes it challenging to convince shippers.
Tseng mentioned that red tape and documentation are significant issues in China, but improvements are being made.
Martinair became the first European airline authorized to fly scheduled services into Guangzhou after delays in October and November.
Martinair plans to start regular scheduled services on January 23 and continue every Friday thereafter.
China Southern Airlines has also received permission to begin its first European service to Amsterdam.

A bank may face a crisis if all its customers were dead on Jan. 1, 2000.
The 'millennium bug' raises concerns about dependence on the financial system.
Predictions about the millennium bug include potential destruction of the financial system.
The issue arises from computers representing the year in two digits instead of four.
British banking officials claim the system will be 'millennium-compatible' by the end of 1998.
There is vagueness in responses regarding preparations for the millennium bug.
If unresolved, computers may misinterpret Jan. 1, 2000, as Jan. 1, 1900.
NatWest plans to spend up to 100 million British pounds to address the issue.
Banking systems must interrelate with other banks and companies.
Computers in stores have already begun to malfunction with credit cards expiring after 1999.

Glaxo Wellcome Plc reported an 18 percent increase in pre-tax profit for 1996.
The company's pre-tax profits rose to 2.964 billion pounds from 2.505 billion pounds.
Sales increased by nine percent to 8.341 billion pounds.
Shareholders received a 13 percent increase in the dividend to 34.0 pence.
Glaxo Wellcome anticipates flat profits for 1997 and 1998 due to a decline in Zantac sales.
The company's shares rose by 11-1/2 pence to 10.48 pounds despite early falls.
Analysts expressed confidence in Glaxo Wellcome's management performance.
Glaxo Wellcome predicts a return to double-digit sales growth in 1999.
The company plans to launch 20 new products over the next four years.
Sales of Zantac decreased by 14 percent last year but remained the world's biggest-selling drug.

Colombia's lower house of Congress approved a law that will almost triple maximum jail terms for drug traffickers.
The bill was passed unanimously without debate.
The Senate approved the bill late on Tuesday.
The law is set to be enacted after presidential signature by next week.
The vote is likely to please the United States.
The legislation raises the maximum jail term for drug-related crimes to 60 years from the current maximum of 24.
Legislator Roy Barreras stated that the law represents the toughest anti-drug penalties in Colombian history.
Barreras denounced U.S. pressure to rush the law through Congress.
President Bill Clinton is scheduled to announce on February 27 whether Colombia should be certified as a trustworthy ally in the drug war.
Justice Minister Carlos Medellin stated that Colombia produces strong laws to combat drug trafficking and crime.

Pier 1 Imports is targeting earnings growth near the high end of its annual objective of 15 to 18 percent for the year.
Chief Executive Clark Johnson stated that the company has an internal goal to exceed this range, but it is not a forecast.
Raymond James projects Pier 1 will report fiscal 1997 earnings of $1.25 per share, a 19 percent increase from $1.05 for fiscal 1996.
Pier 1 projects sales will rise by about $100 million this year.
The company has 725 stores in North America and joint ventures in England, Mexico, and Japan.
Pier 1 posted fiscal 1996 sales of $944.6 million.
The company plans to open 53 stores and close about 25 this year.
Remodeling and remerchandising of store layouts is underway throughout much of the chain.
Pier 1 stopped selling apparel at the end of its fiscal year last month.
The company is enhancing its home furnishings offerings in response to changing consumer attitudes.

Music companies are waiting for a new sound to entice consumers back into record shops.
Analysts expect that without new global best sellers and an economic upturn, global sales will not see double digit growth.
Global sales of pre-recorded music reached $39.8 billion in 1996.
The growth in retail value of global sales was 5.5 percent over 1995.
Four billion compact discs, cassettes, and records were sold in 1996, which is four percent more than in 1995.
The rate of growth in retail value was six percent in 1995 and 15 percent in 1994.
Growth in developing markets is surging, while mature markets like North America have static sales and falling prices.
David Chermont, a media analyst at Merrill Lynch, stated that investors have become accustomed to a lack of significant growth.
Another unnamed analyst suggested that the industry could see significant growth if a new sound emerges.
In 1996, around 70 percent of the world's music growth was generated in less developed markets, particularly in Latin America and Asia.

Toronto's stock market ended mixed on Friday.
The Toronto Stock Exchange's key 300 Composite Index dipped 2.35 points to reach 5826.27.
Turnover was 78 million shares worth C$1.1 billion.
The market added nearly 150 points from its opening level of 5676.39 on Monday.
The market rose 30 points on Thursday.
Dunnery Best is the director of private client investing at Midland Walwyn.
Of Toronto's 14 sub-indices, eight rose and six lost ground.
Base metals, transportation, and forestry products were among the gaining groups.
Consumer products, golds, and media were among the weak groups.
Advancing issues outnumbered decliners 504 to 422, while 279 traded flat.

Russia's upcoming harvest will be slightly better than last year's poor level.
Viktor Khlystun is the agriculture minister of Russia.
Khlystun stated that Russia would produce at least 70 million net tonnes of grain this year.
Moscow will not need to import wheat this year according to Khlystun.
Khlystun expressed hope that the grain production would exceed 70 million tonnes.
Seventy percent of Russian farms are on the verge of collapse.
Khlystun is a newly appointed deputy prime minister and represents the farm lobby.
A government program aims to stabilize and reform the agricultural sector.
Ten to fifteen percent of farms are described as chronically broke and lacking vision.
Russian grain output has decreased by approximately 40 percent from peak levels.

Microsoft Chairman Bill Gates stated that French President Jacques Chirac was reluctant to allow private companies to use highly encrypted code for messages and transactions on the Internet.
Gates mentioned that there was a problem with the U.S. government and now a second one with France.
Gates expressed that strong encryption should be allowed in France.
Encryption makes messages and transactions safe on the Internet but complicates tracking by authorities.
Gates discussed education with Chirac and emphasized the importance of computer literacy for future competitiveness.
Gates claimed that the gap in Internet use between the United States and Europe in ten years would be significant.
Gates' private foundation will support European school computer projects, with the first French projects expected in 1997.
Gates stated that he wanted to spend most of his wealth on projects and charity, claiming that ninety-five percent of his wealth would be returned to society.
Gates indicated that future Microsoft products would focus on simplicity to enhance usability.
Jean-Philippe Courtois of Microsoft France reported that France ranked ninth in the number of Internet users and web sites.

Microsoft Corp is expected to show a 40 percent increase in quarterly earnings.
The increase is attributed to the strength of Microsoft's core business and the latest upgrade to its Office suite.
Analysts expect Microsoft to post earnings of $0.64 a share for its fiscal third quarter.
This is an increase from $0.44 a year ago after adjusting for a split.
Analysts predict revenues in the range of $2.9 billion, up about 32 percent from last year's $2.2 billion.
Microsoft launched Office 97 in January, which is part of its productivity applications.
Office applications accounted for an estimated $2 billion of Microsoft's $8.7 billion in fiscal 1996 revenues.
Microsoft generates about a third of its revenues from operating systems preloaded on new personal computers.
Rick Sherlund of Goldman Sachs estimated that Microsoft's BackOffice business would be up 100 percent over the year-earlier quarter.
Analysts expect growth to slow in the fiscal year beginning July 1.

Miami is known as the cruise-ship capital of the world.
Business in Miami is experiencing high booking levels.
The Walt Disney Co. is preparing to enter the cruise market.
Disney currently operates hotels and theme parks, including Disney World in Orlando.
Disney is considered a leading competitor for vacation spending in the cruise industry.
Disney is offering week-long cruises from Port Canaveral, Florida, on themed ships.
Disney's cruises include stays at its parks and a visit to a Disney island in the Bahamas.
Disney is taking bookings for cruises starting in April 1998.
Industry executives believe Disney will positively impact the entire cruise market.
Carnival Corp. holds 26.9 percent of the global cruise market share.

Rural U.S. wireless firms expect to continue rapid growth without significant competition from Personal Communications Services (PCS) rivals.
John Stanton is the chief executive of Western Wireless Corp.
CommNet Cellular Inc, 360 Communications Co, Palmer Wireless Inc, and Vanguard Cellular Systems Inc expect to benefit from the lack of PCS competition.
Steven Yanis is an analyst at Salomon Bros.
Wireless stocks have been depressed throughout the year despite increases in subscriber numbers, revenues, and cash flows.
Fears of competition from aggressive PCS companies have impacted wireless stock performance.
By 1999, there will be five wireless competitors in most big city markets instead of two.
David Roddy is the chief telecommunications economist at Deloitte and Touche Consulting.
Population density is critical in understanding competitive threats in the wireless market.
CommNet Cellular reported almost 60 percent growth in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization in the year ending June.

Hong Kong's democracy movement compared Beijing's plans to limit civil liberties to the Cultural Revolution from 1966 to 1976.
The pro-democracy camp held a protest at the office of Tung Chee-hwa on Friday morning.
Protesters shouted slogans advocating for the protection of freedom of assembly and association.
Some protesters wore tall hats and labels reminiscent of the Cultural Revolution's political persecution.
Pro-democracy activists are opposing plans to amend or eliminate 25 laws in Hong Kong on July 1.
Laws targeted for amendment include parts of the Bill of Rights and laws related to freedom of assembly and association.
The Hong Kong group organized a sit-down protest outside the Xinhua News Agency branch office.
Other protests were scheduled for Sunday.
Yeung Sum, deputy leader of the Democratic Party, expressed concerns about Hong Kong's autonomy after the handover.
Democratic Party leader Martin Lee planned a news conference and an eight-nation tour to advocate for human rights in Hong Kong.

Pratt & Whitney opened a regional office in Paris to support a new market strategy.
The Paris office is located in the La Defense business district.
The new strategy aims to get closer to civil and military clients.
Robert Wolfe is the president of large commercial engines at Pratt & Whitney.
Pratt & Whitney has a 53 percent share of engines sold for the Airbus A330.
Pratt & Whitney has a 41 percent share of engines sold for the Boeing 777.
The company aims to manage all aspects of the propulsion system for airlines.
The engine overhaul business is expected to generate $1.0 billion to $1.5 billion by the end of next year.
Pratt & Whitney is discussing the thrust management concept with British Airways, Swissair, and Singapore Airlines.
Pratt & Whitney is considering acquisitions and joint ventures to enhance operations.

President Bill Clinton pressured the nation's distillers to stop advertising hard liquor on the airwaves.
The distillers urged President Clinton to gather the beer, wine, and spirits industries to develop a common advertising code.
The White House showed little enthusiasm for the distillers' proposal.
The wine and beer industries rejected the idea of a common advertising code.
The Wine Institute stated that common usage indicates that all drinks are not the same.
The Distilled Spirits Council of the United States (DISCUS) wrote a letter to President Clinton urging him to facilitate a meeting of the industries and broadcasters.
DISCUS requested the development and adoption of a common code for alcohol ads within 90 days.
President Clinton asked the Federal Communications Commission to study ways to limit hard liquor advertising on television and radio.
The hard liquor industry abandoned a voluntary ban on advertising last year.
The Beer Institute stated that there are significant differences between beer and hard liquor, making a common advertising code impractical.

Hong Kong's business and political leaders are preparing for challenges after the handover party.
Hong Kong can no longer rely on its role as the gateway to China to maintain its trading economy status.
Tung Chee-hwa stated that improving Hong Kong's competitiveness is an economic challenge.
Hong Kong's leaders believe drastic action is necessary to compete with rival economies.
Tung emphasized the need for Hong Kong to become more compassionate and address issues in education, housing, and elderly care.
Tung claimed that meeting these challenges is essential for sustaining economic vitality and improving quality of life.
Tung's approach to economic and social policy includes addressing 'livelihood' issues.
Hong Kong has HK$330 billion in reserves available for improvement initiatives.
Hong Kong's manufacturing base has shifted from low-value goods to a service-oriented economy.
The contribution of manufacturing to Hong Kong's GDP has decreased to single digits, while services now account for 85 percent of GDP.

Royal & Sun Alliance Group Plc approved a share buyback on Tuesday.
The company reported a 24 percent increase in pre-tax operating profits for the first quarter of 1997.
Pre-tax operating profits for the first three months of the year were 195 million pounds ($320.6 million).
The increase in profits was aided by a fall in weather-related costs in the United States.
Shares of Royal & Sun Alliance slipped back 7-1/2 pence to 482 pence by late morning.
The company aims to achieve at least 175 million pounds in cost savings identified during last year's merger.
Chief executive Richard Gamble stated that brokers can start the buyback process.
A 34 million pound fall in weather-related costs boosted U.S. general business profits to 51 million pounds.
A rise in UK subsidence led to a five million pound drop in British profits to 50 million pounds.
Analysts' views on the stock depend on the pace of progress in integrating operations.

New York state Attorney General Dennis Vacco plans to sue America Online Inc. if negotiations with prosecutors from 20 states break down.
Vacco aims to halt allegedly deceptive business practices and win refunds for frustrated customers of America Online.
Vacco and prosecutors from 20 states met with America Online to discuss complaints from subscribers experiencing access difficulties.
Vacco sent notification of New York state's proposed litigation to America Online's headquarters in Dulles, Va.
The lawsuit would allege that America Online engaged in deceptive sales practices, false advertising, and fraud.
America Online has five business days to respond to the notice of proposed litigation.
Company officials were not available for comment on the potential lawsuit, but America Online stated it was cooperating with the 20 states.
America Online has seen an increase in subscribers and busy signals since switching to a flat-rate pricing plan on December 1.
AOL announced plans to spend $350 million to upgrade its network and requested customers to limit usage during peak hours.
AOL has already faced at least four class-action lawsuits from subscribers.

Whitbread Plc appointed David Thomas as its chief executive designate.
David Thomas will take over from Peter Jarvis, who will step down next summer.
The investment community views Thomas's appointment as a natural progression from the Jarvis era.
Under Peter Jarvis, Whitbread transformed from a brewer to a diversified leisure company in less than six years.
Since 1985, beer accounts for only 14 percent of Whitbread's profits.
The remainder of Whitbread's profits comes from its managed estates, restaurant, and leisure arm.
Analysts expect Thomas to continue expanding Whitbread's leisure and restaurant business.
Charles Winston, an analyst at BZW, stated that Thomas will continue the retail and leisure direction of the company.
A slide in Whitbread shares was attributed to profit-taking rather than disappointment in the new executive appointment.
John Beaumont, an analyst at Merrill Lynch, noted that Thomas's appointment seems like a natural progression for the company.

China's Foreign Minister Qian Qichen dismissed British opposition to Beijing's plans to disband Hong Kong's legislature.
Qian stated that British opposition would not affect the smooth transfer of power in Hong Kong.
Qian described the British opposition as an overreaction, unreasonable, and unnecessary.
Hong Kong is set to revert to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30.
After the transfer of power, Hong Kong will become a Special Administrative Region of China.
Beijing has pledged to allow Hong Kong a high degree of autonomy for 50 years after the transfer of power.
China plans to scrap Hong Kong's existing elected Legislative Council and install an appointed provisional body.
The move to disband the Legislative Council is opposed by Britain and the United States.
Qian stated that no foreign country has the right to interfere in the affairs of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.
Hong Kong will be entitled to 36 seats in China's National People's Congress next year.

The Czech December trade deficit is expected to rise to 16 billion crowns ($575 million) from 14.3 billion in November 1995.
The Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) will release the 1996 trade figures at 9 a.m. (0800 GMT) on Monday.
Most economists surveyed expect steady growth in the trade deficit with few surprises.
Martin Kupka, an economist at Patria Finance, stated that he expects the figures to align with the development throughout 1996.
The full-year trade gap for 1996 is guaranteed to be a record, as the January-November figure reached 140.1 billion crowns.
The 1995 record total shortfall was 95.7 billion crowns.
Most analysts predict a December trade gap of 15-17 billion crowns, following a 16.6 billion crown shortfall in November.
The consensus forecast for the 1996 trade deficit is between 155-165 billion crowns.
The foreign exchange and money markets are expected to show little reaction to the trade figures unless they significantly differ from estimates.
Czech exporters indicated a desire for a 20 to 25 percent devaluation of the crown to boost exports in 1997.

China is involved in a dispute between North Korea and South Korea.
A North Korean official, Hwang Jang-yop, is seeking asylum at the South Korean embassy in Beijing.
South Korea claims that Hwang Jang-yop and an assistant are seeking asylum.
North Korea accused South Korea of kidnapping Hwang Jang-yop.
North Korea urged China to resolve the situation in its favor.
Diplomats believe it is unlikely for China to resolve the dispute without disappointing North Korea.
Hwang Jang-yop is one of 11 secretaries on the secretariat of North Korea's ruling Workers' Party.
South Korea sent Kim Ha-jung to Beijing for discussions regarding Hwang's asylum.
Chinese police blocked access to South Korea's consular office in Beijing for security reasons.
Hwang Jang-yop is the highest-ranking North Korean official to seek asylum in South Korea.

Brierley Investments Ltd is an investment group based in New Zealand.
Brierley Investments Ltd called on the Australian government to relax its investment rules.
Brierley Investments Ltd wants New Zealand companies to be treated the same as Australian companies in terms of investment.
Brierley chairman Bob Matthew stated that Australia should change its rules to allow New Zealand investment into Australia.
Matthew expressed that there is no merit in having one market for trade and two distinct markets for investment in Australasia.
Brierley Investments has made major investments in Australian companies over the last two to three years.
Brierley Investments owns 28 percent of James Hardie Industries Ltd, 7.4 percent of Coles Myer Ltd, and 19.9 percent of John Fairfax Holdings Ltd.
Brierley Investments has A$1.8 billion invested in Australia and A$1.6 billion in New Zealand.
