Brierley Investments faced restrictions that stalled its investment push in Australia this year.
Matthew indicated that he is not optimistic about the Australian government changing its investment regulations.

Strippers can dance naked in Canada as long as they maintain distance from customers.
The Supreme Court of Canada ruled that lap dancing is indecent and a criminal act.
Exotic dancers cheered the Supreme Court ruling that bans lap dancing.
Club owners warned that the ban on lap dancing could deter customers and harm businesses.
A dancer at Filmores stated that dancing is for seeing, not touching.
Andy, a patron at the Zanzibar strip club, claimed the court ban on lap dancing was unnecessary.
Lap dancing became widespread in Canada after a 1994 Ontario judge's ruling that it did not offend community standards.
Katharine Goldberg, a former stripper, led a campaign against lap dancing, claiming it forced dancers into degrading acts.
Some strippers expressed resentment towards Goldberg's portrayal of them as sex slaves.
The Supreme Court upheld an appeal court decision that stated lap dancing degraded dancers and encouraged objectification.

Britain could raise between 600 million and 1.5 billion pounds from the sale of the London Underground rail network, according to Steven Norris.
Steven Norris is a former transport minister and is currently working on the Conservative Party election manifesto.
Norris is leading the Conservative Party's election campaign for London and the south-east of England.
Norris stated that the government is examining fare and service standard controls for the tube network.
Norris has been involved informally with government studies regarding a possible sale of the tube network.
The sale proceeds figure mentioned by Norris excludes the cost of necessary investments.
The gross proceeds figure for the sale of the tube network is estimated to be between 1.4 billion and 2.5 billion pounds.
London Underground has become a significant political issue in the lead-up to Britain's general election.
There is pressure on the government to present a compelling case to the public regarding the sale of the tube.
Labour leader Tony Blair has stated his commitment to keeping the tube in public hands and revitalizing it through private sector investment.

Two troubled banks in Japan took action on Tuesday to address financial issues.
Nippon Credit Bank Ltd announced a radical restructuring.
Nippon Credit Bank Ltd will cease overseas operations and sell its Tokyo headquarters.
Nippon Credit Bank Ltd will write off bad loans totaling 460 billion yen ($3.7 billion).
Nippon Credit Bank Ltd expects the restructuring to boost earnings by 50 billion yen ($403 million) over five years.
Nippon Credit Bank Ltd hopes to gain 67 billion yen ($540 million) from real estate sales.
Nippon Credit Bank Ltd will eliminate 600 jobs to cut costs.
The Japanese government is taking steps to ensure Nippon Credit Bank Ltd survives.
Hokkaido Takushoku Bank announced it will merge with Hokkaido Bank Ltd.
Hokkaido Takushoku Bank will cease overseas operations to become a 'super-regional' bank.

Canada's political leaders are campaigning for re-election on June 2.
Political leaders are accusing each other of being too American in their approach to Canada's health care system.
Canada's universal medicare plan has faced significant cuts in recent years due to efforts to reduce deficits.
All main political parties in Canada are pledging to reinvest in health care if successful on June 2.
Alexa McDonough, leader of the New Democrats, claims that the ruling Liberals and Conservative and Reform parties want to cut health care.
McDonough argues that these cuts are pushing Canada closer to an American-style two-tiered health care system.
Government-funded universal health care is considered a key aspect of Canadian identity.
Polls indicate that the preservation of health care is a major concern in the upcoming election.
The Liberals have reduced health and education spending to C$12.5 billion, down from C$18.5 billion in 1993.
The Liberals claim to defend universal medicare principles by preventing extra charges from doctors and hospitals.

A Czech cabinet decision will require deposits on consumer goods imports.
Analysts believe the deposit requirement will be less harmful for inflation than import surcharges.
The deposit requirement may have little impact on the trade deficit.
The government plans to cut public sector wage growth to 7.3 percent this year from 11.9 percent.
Analysts say the wage growth cut will be more effective in reducing demand for imported products than the deposit programme.
The deposit programme will come into effect on Monday.
Importers will be required to deposit 20 percent of the value of imported consumer goods for 180 days.
Commercial banks will channel the deposit money to state-held development bank Konsolidacni Banka.
Industry and Trade Minister Vladimir Dlouhy announced the new measure and hopes it will reverse the widening trade deficit.
The deposits will apply to about 30 percent of imports, including foodstuffs, cars, electronics, textiles, furniture, and appliances.

Air Canada is interested in opening new Asian destinations including Tokyo and Singapore.
Lamar Durrett is the president and chief executive officer of Air Canada.
Durrett spoke to the Canadian Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong.
The Canadian Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong is reputed to be the largest outside Canada.
Air Canada is looking forward to future competition with Asian carriers.
Air Canada hopes to benefit from open skies agreements.
Air Canada is positioning itself for a major expansion of services in the Asia-Pacific region.
Durrett stated that trade and travel links between Asia, Europe, and North America are increasing.
There has been a 41 percent increase in trans-Pacific capacity with Air Canada's winter schedule.
Air Canada currently flies to Osaka in partnership with ANA.

The Halifax Building Society is Britain's largest home loan lender.
In 1996, the Halifax posted a 6.6 percent rise in pre-tax profits to 1.43 billion pounds.
The Halifax is expected to float for around 12 billion pounds after converting from mutual status.
The Halifax hinted at further acquisitions to increase its 20 percent share of the total mortgage market.
Mike Blackburn is the chief executive of the Halifax.
Blackburn stated that the Halifax could increase its market share to 25 percent before attracting attention from the Office of Fair Trading.
The Halifax is not currently engaged in any acquisition discussions.
British competition authorities typically investigate proposed mergers if more than 25 percent of a market is involved.
The Halifax is unlikely to acquire another mutually-owned life assurance company after purchasing Clerical Medical.
Blackburn believes that long-term savings products have strong growth potential due to an ageing population.

Clyde Petroleum Plc is considering an improved offer of 120 pence per share from Gulf Canada Resources.
Shareholders of Clyde Petroleum Plc are disappointed that Gulf Canada Resources did not make a more compelling offer.
Key shareholders may wait for a rival bidder to emerge in the next two weeks.
Clyde's share price remained at 120 pence during Tuesday afternoon trading.
Analysts believe Clyde's share price is influenced by the potential for another bid and the possibility of large shareholders accepting Gulf's offer.
Gulf Canada's final proposal values Clyde Petroleum Plc at 494.6 million pounds ($793 million).
Gulf Canada's offer represents a 14 percent increase from its original offer of 105 pence made on December 18.
The offer is a 42 percent premium to Clyde's share price before the bid was announced.
Clyde Petroleum Plc rejected Gulf Canada's latest bid, stating it is worth more than the offered price.
Gulf Canada's president J.P. Bryan stated there has been no indication of a rival offer.

Marjorie Scardino is the new chief executive of Pearson Plc.
Marjorie Scardino is the first woman to head a major British company.
Pearson announced a 1996 operating profit of 281 million pounds.
The operating profit of 281 million pounds represents a rise of eight percent.
Pearson took a 100 million pound charge for improper accounting at its Penguin USA subsidiary.
Finance Director John Makinson does not expect Pearson to increase the provision for problems at Penguin USA.
The issues at Penguin USA date back to 1991.
Pearson increased its full year dividend to 18p from 16.5p.
Pearson's shares slipped 9p to 765p in early trading.
Scardino plans to focus on performance and may change the business strategy over time.

The boards of RightChoice Managed Care Inc and Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Missouri are working to improve relations with regulators.
The boards aim to return to profitability and ensure control remains with chief executive John O'Rourke.
Talks about a possible combination of RightChoice and BJC Health Systems have been halted.
The project to combine RightChoice and BJC Health Systems was initiated by two executives who were fired.
John O'Rourke stated that the talks with BJC were called off primarily for business reasons.
O'Rourke indicated that the proposed deal would not be acceptable to the national Blue Cross association.
The boards of RightChoice and the Missouri Blues expressed support for O'Rourke.
RightChoice expects to return to profitability by the third or fourth quarter of the year.
RightChoice reported a loss of $3.7 million on revenues of $170.2 million in the fourth quarter.
The Missouri Blues sued the Missouri Department of Insurance director in May 1996 regarding the restructuring of RightChoice.

Japan's Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp is in talks with France's Cie Generale des Eaux about taking a stake in its French railway venture.
A CGE unit confirmed the talks on Tuesday.
NTT is considering a 9.9 percent stake in CGE's railway venture, Telecom Developpement.
CGE's subsidiary Cegetel is majority-owned by CGE and is France's second telecoms operator.
BT is investing 1.1 billion pounds ($1.8 billion) to take a 25 percent stake in Cegetel.
Cegetel can take a stake of up to 49.9 percent in Telecom Developpement.
Cegetel might limit its holding to 40 percent and seek a minority partner for the balance.
BT and its U.S. partner MCI Communications Corp have been trying to gain a foothold in Asian markets.
NTT is looking to make its first foreign investment in the French telecom market.
Cegetel was selected to run a network owned by Societe Nationale des Chemins de Fer via Telecom Developpement.

Toronto's stock market reached its eighth record close of 1997.
The Toronto Stock Exchange's 300 Composite Index increased by 60.40 points to close at 6225.78.
The Toronto Stock Exchange set a new intra-day record of 6225.83 points.
Ron Meisels, a Montreal-based portfolio consultant, stated that the market has made a major break to all-time high levels.
Turnover on the Toronto Stock Exchange was 122 million shares worth C$2 billion ($1.48 billion).
New York's stock market gained 60.81 points to close at 7022.44.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average surpassed the 7000 level due to optimism about the U.S. economy, low inflation, and stable interest rates.
Toronto's stock market rose significantly due to increasing bullion prices in London and ongoing merger activity in the oil and gas sector.
All of Toronto's 14 sub-indices increased except for real estate.
Morrison Petroleums Ltd. was the target of a C$652 million ($482 million) hostile takeover by Canadian 88 Energy Corp. but announced a merger with Northstar Energy Corp.

Russian oil producers are trying to gain control over a portion of the country's crude oil exports.
Traders are concerned that their favorable position in Russia's oil market may be declining.
New Russian oil majors are integrating vertically to gain more control over foreign deliveries.
These oil majors claim they need profits from traders to invest in domestic production and expansion.
Russian and Western traders have more experience with logistics and contacts with Western buyers.
Traders are better equipped to handle changes in the export schedule set by Transneft.
The competition is focused on state-sponsored exports known as federal programmes.
Federal programmes are valued at $2-$3 billion annually and allow companies to export oil with reduced taxes and tariffs.
Traders accounted for 23 percent of Russia's oil exports outside the Commonwealth of Independent States last year.
Russian oil production totaled 6.03 million barrels per day.

Francis Ona is the secessionist rebel leader of Bougainville.
Ona fears that mining will destroy Bougainville if it does not gain independence from Papua New Guinea.
Ona believes Papua New Guinea will allow foreign miners to exploit Bougainville's resources.
Papua New Guinea announced plans to buy back foreign interests in the Panguna copper mine.
The Panguna mine was closed in 1989 after sabotage attacks by rebels.
Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan stated that the buy-back scheme would provide financial compensation to landowners.
The development of the Panguna mine increased secessionist sentiment among Bougainvilleans.
The Panguna mine produced 160,000 tonnes of copper concentrate annually since its opening in 1972.
Ona stated that if independence is not achieved, the Panguna mine and four other mines will be restarted.
Papua New Guinea has hired Sandline International to train troops for a mission to Bougainville.

Boeing announced on Monday that it has scrapped plans to build a new version of its 747 jumbo jet.
Boeing cited current market conditions as the reason for scrapping the 747 plans, stating they do not justify the estimated risk and expense of over $7 billion.
Boeing will focus its development efforts on new versions of its medium-sized 767 and 777 twinjets.
The decision to cancel the 747-X program ends over three years of research, including a joint study with Airbus Industrie.
The proposed double-decker jet from Boeing was intended to accommodate 600 to 800 passengers.
Airbus is now the only company proposing a new superjumbo plane that could seat 600 passengers.
The current-generation 747-400 typically seats 416 passengers in a three-class configuration.
Analysts have expressed skepticism about Airbus's ability to secure funding for its superjumbo, the A-3XX.
Airbus executives estimate the cost to build the A-3XX at $7 billion, while industry sources estimate it closer to $15 billion.
Boeing's decision to scale back the 747-X program will make it more difficult for Airbus to convince investors to fund the A-3XX.

Philip Morris Cos. Inc. Chief Executive Geoffrey Bible stated that the company is open to reasonable measures to resolve anti-tobacco lawsuits in the United States.
Bible declined to comment on negotiations between cigarette companies and anti-smoking forces regarding a resolution of lawsuits and regulations.
Bible expressed willingness to work with government officials on new regulations for tobacco sales.
Philip Morris is currently involved in a court battle against new restrictions on tobacco sales imposed by the Food and Drug Administration.
Bible indicated that Philip Morris supports restrictions on young people purchasing cigarettes.
Philip Morris launched a program two years ago to limit cigarette access for individuals under 21.
Bible stated that Philip Morris does not want children to smoke.
Anti-smoking groups claim that the tobacco industry targets advertising to encourage youth smoking.
Philip Morris shareholders rejected a proposal to adopt marketing standards for youths outside the United States.
Tobacco executives have recently met with state officials and anti-smoking activists to discuss settling litigation against the industry.

AT&T Corp. reported a 14 percent increase in operating profits from continuing operations for the last quarter of 1996.
AT&T set aside $200 million to cover unpaid bills by customers.
AT&T earned $1.24 billion, or 76 cents a share, in the last quarter of 1996.
In the last quarter of 1995, AT&T earned $1.09 billion, or 68 cents a share.
Richard Miller, AT&T's chief financial officer, stated that results for the first quarter of 1997 would be comparable or slightly above those of the fourth quarter.
Revenues for AT&T in the latest quarter rose to $13.24 billion from $12.89 billion.
AT&T's fourth-quarter operating profits in 1995 excluded restructuring and other charges totaling $2.036 billion, or $1.27 a share.
Including these charges, AT&T's net earnings from continuing operations resulted in a loss of $948 million, or 59 cents a share.
Competition has led to challenges for AT&T, particularly with business users and long-distance resellers.
AT&T's fourth-quarter operating net per share was three cents below the 79 cents forecast by industry analysts.

Hong Kong's Democratic Party leaders launched a mission to North America and Europe to brief the West on Hong Kong's situation as China takes over.
Britain will hand Hong Kong back to Beijing at midnight on June 30 after over 150 years of colonial rule.
The Democratic Party has been involved in political clashes with China regarding plans to limit democracy and civil rights in Hong Kong.
Party leader Martin Lee and deputy Szeto Wah will lead the mission to the United States, Canada, and the United Nations offices in Switzerland.
Legislator Andrew Cheng will also participate in the mission.
The mission will include speaking engagements in cities such as Seattle, Vancouver, Calgary, Los Angeles, Sacramento, San Francisco, Boston, Chicago, Toronto, Washington, New York, Ottawa, and Geneva.
This tour is the largest undertaken by the Hong Kong democratic movement to advocate for the protection of basic freedoms in the territory.
Martin Lee is in opposition to both China and Tung Chee-hwa, who is the chosen leader for Hong Kong by Beijing.
Lee plans to testify at the United Nations Human Rights Commission in Geneva on April 7 about threats to freedom and civil rights in Hong Kong.
China intends to roll back liberal laws regarding freedom of association and assembly, and plans to dissolve Hong Kong's elected Legislative Council after the handover.

The Czech Republic reached the final of Euro '96.

Talks between Caterpillar Inc. and the United Auto Workers will resume with the help of a federal mediator.

China suggested to Guatemala that it should sever ties with Taiwan to persuade Beijing to lift its U.N. veto.

Rains favouring Ivorian cocoa midcrop development ended abruptly in early February.

Hicks, Muse, Tate & Furst Inc will soon own Chef Boyardee, Polaner fruit spreads, and PAM cooking spray.

Hewlett-Packard Co. plans to introduce a photographic system for personal computer users.

Tung Chee-hwa is the future leader of Hong Kong.

Wall Street's interest in International Business Machines Corp (IBM) decreased after its disappointing fourth quarter earnings.

Labour leader Tony Blair supported a public-private partnership for the metro system.
Blair stated that the partnership would provide an alternative to wholesale privatisation.
Shadow transport secretary Andrew Smith shifted away from the interventionist policies of his predecessor Clare Short.
Labour's revised transport vision promised tougher regulation without reversing the rail sell-off.
Smith proposed using the private sector for investment in track maintenance and new trains.
Labour plans to push policies for less road building and more traffic management.

Japan's securities watchdog, the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC), is investigating Nomura Securities Co Ltd for possibly illegal deals.
The investigation has been ongoing since September and focuses on how Nomura provided profits to a corporate customer.
A government source indicated that the investigation is unlikely to conclude quickly and may take at least a few more weeks.
The source urged Nomura to cooperate fully with the investigation.
Nomura has not been as cooperative as authorities had hoped until recently.
Under the Securities and Exchange Law, the SESC can recommend administrative punishment if illegal activity is found.
The heaviest penalty under the law could include revocation of brokerage licenses and suspension of business for up to six months.
The SESC can also refer the case to prosecutors for legal action.
Nomura acknowledged that two of its directors engaged in transactions that were deemed 'discretionary' and violated Japan's securities law.
Media reports have connected Nomura to a former 'sokaiya' racketeer, but the company could not confirm these reports.

Inco Ltd. has closed its C$4.3 billion takeover of Diamond Fields Resources Inc.
The acquisition gives Inco a significant role in the nickel market.
The Voisey's Bay deposit is located in Labrador, Canada.
Diamond Fields shareholders could choose between common shares in Inco, cash, preferred shares, or VBN shares.
Inco paid out the full C$350 million in cash to shareholders.
Inco distributed 50.3 million common shares, 25.9 million VBN shares, and 9.4 million preferred shares as part of the acquisition.
Inco's bid for Diamond Fields beat out rival Falconbridge Ltd.
A lawsuit against Diamond Fields executives and Inco was settled on August 5.
The Voisey's Bay deposit is estimated to contain about 150 million metric tons of ore.
Inco must negotiate with local native groups and obtain environmental approvals before starting production.

A hardline Chinese magazine has criticized Wang Meng, a prominent author and former culture minister.
The criticism appears in the January issue of the magazine Zhongliu, or Mainstay.
The article is written under the pen-name Gong Yizhou.
The article claims that Wang Meng has failed to support the rule of the Communist Party.
The article accuses Wang Meng of not adequately opposing bourgeois liberalism.
The article questions whether Wang Meng's actions meet the basic requirements of a party member.
The article states that Wang Meng has not written a self-criticism regarding his mistakes.
The article claims that Wang Meng played a negative role in supporting the 1989 pro-democracy demonstrations.
Wang Meng was appointed minister of culture in 1986 and removed from the position in August 1989.
The article is considered one of the fiercest attacks against an individual mentioned by name in recent years in China.

The British government is unlikely to block CE Electric's 650 pence per share bid for Northern Electric on competition grounds.
Concerns exist that Trade Secretary Ian Lang might block the takeover for political reasons.
Lang is expected to announce his decision by December 16.
CE Electric has set a self-imposed deadline of December 20 for acceptances of its bid.
Northern's shares were down 3.5 pence at 598 pence by 1400 GMT.
CE Electric raised its original 630 pence offer to 650 pence on December 6.
CE Electric has acquired just under 30 percent of Northern Electric on the market.
Approval of the Northern bid would leave three independent regional electricity companies out of an original 12.
East Midlands Electricity postponed its half-year results until after the decision on Northern.
CE Electric is 70 percent owned by CalEnergy.

Interest rates on British home loans may rise this year due to upward pressure on savings rates.
Analysts stated that this potential rise is separate from the government's monetary policy decisions after the general election on May 1.
The flotation of four building societies and the takeover of another will release up to 140 billion pounds of savings from nearly 30 million accounts.
This amount represents around 25 percent of British retail savings.
Analysts expect a significant portion of this released savings to be moved.
UBS building societies analyst Rob Thomas estimated that 15 billion pounds would be moved as a conservative estimate.
The movement of savings is expected to push up savings rates and put pressure on mortgage margins.
Halifax, Woolwich, Alliance & Leicester, and Northern Rock are ending their mutual society status and floating on the stock market.
Savers in these building societies had to deposit money to qualify for free shares, but can move their money after the floatation.
Abbey National and Cheltenham & Gloucester are expected to compete for the released funds.

Britain's science base is deteriorating, affecting future investment in the pharmaceutical industry.
Major companies, including Glaxo Wellcome Plc and SmithKline Beecham Plc, have expressed concerns about this issue.
George Poste, chairman of research and development at SmithKline Beecham, warned that the decline in graduate training and education quality could lead to research being conducted abroad.
Poste stated that a society that does not keep up scientifically risks becoming a second-tier nation.
Concerns stem from a push over the past decade to increase the number of 18-year-olds in higher education, which companies believe is lowering standards.
Michael Elves, director of scientific and educational affairs at Glaxo Wellcome, noted that graduates often lack adequate numeracy, literacy, and computer skills.
The industry is also facing a shortage of basic laboratory experience due to outdated equipment and high student numbers.
Poste mentioned that the need for up to two years of remedial training is a hidden tax on the industry.
Both Glaxo Wellcome and SmithKline Beecham have made significant investments in research facilities in Britain.
SmithKline Beecham has already moved some operations to the United States due to skill shortages.

Mirror Group Plc posted a pre-tax profit increase of 2.9 percent to 39.0 million pounds in the first six months of the year.
The interim dividend was increased to 1.35p from 1.2p.
Initial market reaction to the profit increase was positive, with Mirror shares rising by seven to 208.5p.
Chief executive David Montgomery stated that Mirror Group has outperformed other newspaper companies in absorbing a 35 percent increase in newsprint costs.
Montgomery claimed that Mirror Group maintained high levels of marketing investment and still produced an increase in profits.
Mirror Group's flagship title is the Daily Mirror, which is Britain's second-top selling newspaper.
Mirror Group has a major stake in The Independent and has recently branched out into cable television.
Newsprint costs rose by 18 million pounds year-on-year, but Mirror Group managed to offset this through higher advertising and circulation revenues.
Finance Director John Allwood reported that cover price rises boosted circulation revenue by 11 million pounds and advertising revenue increased by around five million.
The Mirror's Television arm reported losses of 4.2 million pounds due to start-up costs at its Live TV local cable service.

Qantas Airways Ltd reported a 2.4 percent rise in net profit for the 1996/97 first half.
Qantas warned that its Japan routes were unlikely to repeat the profitability of the early 1990s.
Qantas is 25 percent owned by British Airways Plc.
Qantas reported a net profit of A$151.6 million for the six months ended December 31.
The reported net profit was towards the higher end of market expectations.
Qantas aimed to at least match the A$246.2 million net profit recorded in the full 1995/96 fiscal year.
The growth in profit was largely due to Qantas's cost cutting programme.
Qantas has cut costs by over A$1.0 billion in the past three years.
Sales rose 2.5 percent to A$3.97 billion for the fiscal half-year.
Revenue from Japan fell about 30 percent to A$315 million in the first half.

Sybase Inc. will revamp its flagship database software product and other programmes this year.
Chief Executive Officer Mitchell Kertzman announced the changes on Wednesday.
An improved version of SQL Server System 11 will be released by the second or third quarter.
The new lineup will include development tools for easier information storage and retrieval in corporate databases.
Sybase has been struggling in the past two years due to competition from Oracle Corp., Informix Corp., and Microsoft Corp.
Kertzman has trimmed Sybase's product lines and cut hundreds of jobs to focus on the core database business.
Kertzman stated that customers wanted a cohesive product offering rather than unrelated software.
Sybase plans to release a test version of the improved System 11, code-named 11G, soon.
The improved System 11 will have better performance in parallel systems to compete with Informix.
Sybase will also release a product code-named 'Jaguar,' a transaction server for easier data retrieval.

Toronto stocks finished one percent higher on Tuesday.
The increase followed a rally in New York.
Investors speculated that the U.S. central bank may not raise interest rates.
This speculation was based on surprisingly weak U.S. economic data.
The Toronto Stock Exchange's key 300 Composite Index rose 67.98 points to close at 5903.56.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 179 points to finish at 6962.
Ira Katzin, an investment advisor with RBC Dominion Securities, stated that economic stats suggest the economy is slowing down.
The U.S. employment cost index rose 0.6 percent in the first quarter.
Economists had expected a 0.9 percent increase in the employment cost index.
April's index of U.S. consumer confidence dipped to 116.8 from 118.5 in March.

Russia's Norilsk Nickel metals group expressed a desire to be a competitive company.
Norilsk Nickel does not want to be a financial supporter of the Arctic.
RAO Norilsky Nickel spokesman Sergei Vetchinin stated that supporting the town of Norilsk is draining company resources.
Vetchinin claimed that the company needs resources to recover from a financial crisis and increase production.
Vetchinin stated that capitalists do not support cities.
Vetchinin mentioned that the city of Norilsk was created for the company.
Vetchinin noted that some parts of the town are not related to the company.
Norilsk is a key producer of nickel and precious metals.
Norilsk is located 200 miles north of the Arctic Circle.
Norilsk Nickel faces challenges in overcoming the legacy of the Soviet Union regarding production costs.

Colonial Ltd made its debut on the Australian share market on Monday.
Colonial shares opened at A$3.31 (US$2.56).
The opening price was above the A$3.10 paid by institutional investors.
The public share offer closed last Friday.
The opening price was higher than the A$2.60 paid by members of the public.
Colonial shares were trading around the opening price in late morning trade.
Colonial had a market capitalisation of A$1.9 billion.
Colonial became the second life office to list on the local exchange.
Peter Smedley is the managing director of Colonial.
Colonial plans to use some float proceeds to develop its life insurance business in Asia.

Ivory Coast opened talks with donors on Monday regarding reform of the cocoa and coffee sector.
The talks aim to qualify for the final part of a loan for agricultural restructuring.
Donors indicated that agreement on releasing the final $45 million of a $150 million loan may not be reached until 1998.
A World Bank official stated that discussions will mainly focus on cocoa and coffee, but some questions may remain unresolved until the end of the year.
The talks are scheduled to conclude on May 7.
Ivory Coast is the world's largest cocoa producer.
Ivory Coast has not released trading data to the World Bank on an export-contract auction established last May.
The World Bank seeks information on volumes, prices, and dates of trades at the auctions.
Agriculture Minister Lambert Kouassi Konan stated that the figures are commercially confidential.
Industry sources have raised concerns that the auction promotes price speculation and overbidding.

A ministerial conference of Mekong River nations took place on Friday.
The conference aimed to promote cross-border cooperation for the development of the region.
Bong-Suh Lee, vice president of the Asian Development Bank (ADB), stated that growing trust among the six nations would facilitate investment.
Lee projected that investment could reach at least $1.3 billion by the turn of the century.
Ministers from Burma, Cambodia, China, Laos, Thailand, and Vietnam agreed to develop infrastructure projects.
The ministers approved strategies for the next 25 years of development along the Mekong River.
The ADB has prepared $300 million in loans for investment in the region over the next three years.
Gunther Hecker of the ADB stated that greater sums would be needed for crucial projects.
Lee indicated that at least $9 billion would be necessary for transport and telecommunications projects in the region.
GMS meetings have been important for building trust among the nations in the region.

OneLink Communications Inc believes it has found a significant opportunity in data mining through telephone calls.
Data mining involves building profiles of customers by aggregating transaction data.
OneLink gathers customer information for various sectors including healthcare, telephone, and real estate.
The company compiles demographic maps that can be used on personal computers.
Nicholas Bluhm is the chief executive of OneLink Communications Inc.
OneLink combines caller information with call management data to build profiles of caller habits.
The company pulls in additional data to obtain household and financial information.
OneLink's initial public offering (IPO) was at $3.50 in April 1995 and closed at $2.25 on a recent Friday.
OneLink lost $1.28 million in the first nine months of 1996, with revenues of $743,000 during that period.
OneLink is transitioning from a hardware-based company to a service-based company.

Deng Xiaoping's death has impacted Hong Kong similarly to Mao Zedong's death in 1976.
Residents of Hong Kong report that the grief following Deng's death is less than that after Mao's death.
Approximately 50,000 people have visited the Xinhua news agency building in Hong Kong to pay respects to Deng since his death.
Some members of the British-ruled community in Hong Kong participated in mourning gestures during Deng's official funeral in Beijing.
During Deng's funeral, ships sounded their horns, buses displayed black ribbons, train stations played somber music, flags were at half mast, and schoolchildren observed a moment of silence.
Deng Xiaoping became China's leader in 1978 after being purged by Mao Zedong.
Deng is credited with opening China to the West and implementing economic reforms.
Mao Zedong died in 1976 after a rule characterized by purges and the Cultural Revolution.
Long-term residents of Hong Kong noted that hundreds of thousands mourned Mao's death.
John Dolfin stated that the turnout for Mao's death was massive compared to Deng's, which was smaller and less emotional.

ITT Corp faces challenges in convincing investors that selling non-core assets is more valuable than Hilton Hotels Corp's $6.5 billion hostile bid.
Wall Street analysts believe ITT would be better focused without assets like Madison Square Garden and world telephone directories.
Shareholders have seen ITT's stock price decline in recent months.
Daniel Davila of Rodman & Redshaw Inc questioned why ITT did not sell assets sooner.
ITT rejected Hilton's $6.5 billion takeover offer, deeming it inadequate and not in the best interest of shareholders.
Hilton Hotels Corp plans to review options to increase shareholder value, including the potential sale of non-core assets.
Industry experts estimate that ITT's non-core assets could generate over $2 billion for stock buybacks or special dividends.
Hilton is expected to raise its offer for ITT, potentially increasing it by up to $10 per share.
Bruce Raabe of Collins & Co stated that a $65 offer from Hilton would make it difficult for ITT to justify rejecting it to shareholders.
Shares of ITT rose by 1-3/4 to 57-3/4 in afternoon trading due to expectations of a higher bid.

E*Trade Group Inc President and Chief Executive Christos Cotsakos stated that the company is increasing its subscribers by eight to ten percent per month.
Cotsakos made this statement during a presentation to investors at Robertson, Stephens & Co's Tech 97 Agenda investment conference.
E*Trade completed its initial public offering in August 1996.
The company's stock closed at a record high of 22-1/8, after reaching an all-time high of 22-7/8 earlier that day.
A deal with Microsoft Corp, which integrates E*Trade's share trading service into Microsoft's online investment service, investor.com, has positively impacted E*Trade's shares.
Analysts believe there is strong potential for continued growth for companies like E*Trade as the Internet expands.
E*Trade averages 550 new accounts per day, representing about $10 million in assets.
On at least one occasion, E*Trade signed up 1,200 new customers in a single day, with assets totaling $22 million.
E*Trade's percentage of total daily retail share trading volume increased from 0.1% in 1995 to 0.7%.
E*Trade processes approximately 7,000 daily transactions over the Internet, which accounts for about half of its total volume.

The Beijing-appointed committee handling Hong Kong's return to Chinese rule completed a two-day session in Beijing.
The committee endorsed China's plans to scrap some civil liberties after the takeover.
Only one of the 150 members of the Preparatory Committee voted against the motion to approve Beijing's plans.
Ten members of the Preparatory Committee abstained from voting.
Frederick Fung, chairman of the Hong Kong Association for Democracy and People's Livelihood, cast the sole dissenting vote.
Fung protested against Beijing's proposed changes in a letter to Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen.
Allen Lee, chairman of the pro-China, pro-business Liberal Party, abstained from the vote.
Tung Chee-hwa, Hong Kong's post-colonial leader, supported the committee's moves.
Tung stated that the liberties of Hong Kong's 6.3 million people are enshrined in the Basic Law.
Beijing's plans to repeal or amend 25 of Hong Kong's laws have prompted protests from Britain and democracy activists.

Lloyd's of London Names are traditional backers of the Lloyd's insurance market.
A working party has been set up to assess the market's funding.
The working party is expected to recommend an increase in the minimum amounts Names provide to support their underwriting.
Lloyd's is expected to announce changes to its capital structure within the next week.
The report from the working party should be published within the next few days.
Currently, Names must provide between 20 and 30 percent of their underwriting capacity as deposits.
Corporate investors must provide 50 percent of their underwriting capacity as deposits.
Under the working party's plans, Names may be required to provide at least 32.5 percent next year and 37.5 percent the following year.
The losses of eight billion pounds between 1988 and 1992 prompted changes in Lloyd's and the introduction of corporate capital.
The number of Names has declined to below 10,000 for the first time since the mid-70s.

America Online Inc. agreed to give some members refunds or credit due to customer complaints and a potential lawsuit.
AOL has 8 million subscribers.
AOL agreed to offer customers a choice of a free month online or up to $39.90 as a refund.
The refund offer was a result of negotiations with state attorneys general.
AOL plans to maintain its membership at 8 million until it can meet current members' needs.
AOL Chairman Steve Case stated the company was working on a refund offer.
Illinois Attorney General Jim Ryan announced a preliminary deal with AOL and 36 states.
Ryan expected AOL to formally sign the agreement by Thursday.
AOL agreed to halt advertising aimed at attracting new customers for a month.
The agreement addresses consumer fraud lawsuits threatened by New York and other states.

Talks aimed at averting a potential auto supplier strike at American Axle & Manufacturing Inc continued on Saturday morning.
Bargainers worked past the midnight Friday deadline.
A person close to the negotiations reported that the negotiators worked through the night and seemed in good spirits.
A strike at American Axle would shut down light truck production at General Motors Corp's 11 North American truck plants within days.
A strike would create supply hardships for Ford Motor Co.
United Auto Workers leaders have not officially extended the strike deadline.
Union members reported that UAW leaders have not authorized members to start picketing.
About 7,200 UAW members were prepared to walk off their jobs at five plants if no agreement was reached on a new three-year contract.
American Axle supplies rear axles for GM's pickup trucks and sport utility vehicles, as well as axles for the Camaro and Firebird.
American Axle also makes axle shafts used by Ford in its F-150 pickup trucks and some rear-drive passenger cars.
